title: Sweden's Riksbank stuns market with bullish comments.
text:
STOCKHOLM, Sept 8 (Reuter) - Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, on Friday took markets by surprise with an upbeat assessment of the country's fight against inflation and even threatened to intervene in the foreign exchange market. 

 Riksbank Deputy Governor Thomas Franzen told Reuters in an interview that Sweden was well on the way to price stability and he saw conditions for a stronger crown and lower market rates. 

 "This is a statement which has to do with our belief that the tone has changed in the market. It is an honest declaration that we do not rule out (the possibility) of reinforcing it," Franzen said. 

 The Swedish crown strengthened around four ore after the report. The 10-year bond traded at 9.72 percent, 25 basis points down on Thursday's close. The crown burst through 4.83 against the mark compared to Thursday's 4.92 close. 

 Franzen also said he saw conditions for a stronger crown and lower market interest rates. 

 "(Our) competitiveness is good, the trade balance is going very well and one senses a better tone when it comes to confidence, the conditions are good," Franzen said. 

 He said he also believed long debt yields could fall. 

 "If inflation indicators keep falling there are also conditions for lower rates," he said. 

 "In effective terms, the crown was strengthening until the middle of July. The trend then stopped. In the past few days the trend has returned, but one naturally does not wish to draw too big conclusions. But the trend is clearly welcome," he said. 

 However, if the crown failed to strengthen sufficiently, he reasserted an earlier Riksbank policy that there was still room for key rate hikes. 

 Franzen added the Riksbank had received queries from the market about possible interventions on the foreign exchange market after recent international interventions on foreign exchange markets. 

Sweden has not intervened to support the crown for about two years.

title: Swedish Riksbank does not rule out  intervention .
text:
STOCKHOLM, Sept 8 (Reuter) - Sweden's Riksbank may in the near future intervene on the foreign exchange market to further reinforce what it calls a "positive trend". 

 "I do not want to rule out that we relatively soon may be in a position to reinforce the positive tone through interventions," Deputy Central Bank Governor Thomas Franzen told Reuters in an interview. 

 Franzen said there was no concrete plan and that interventions could not replace a "decisive monetary policy". 

 "This is a statement which has to do with our belief that the tone has changed in the market. It is an honest declaration that we do not rule out (the possibility) of reinforcing it," Franzen said. 

 Franzen added the Riksbank had received queries from the market about possible intervention on the foreign exchange market after recent international intervention. 

 -- Gran Lind 08-700 1010

title: Intervention  May Provide Some Short-Term Aid For Dollar
text:
LONDON (AP-DJ)--Wednesday's coordinated intervention exercise may provide some short-term support for the dollar against the Deutsche mark and the yen, unlike previous attempts to help the U.S. currency this year. 

 But, market analysts warned, the impact on the market has been largely psychological and the dollar will only be able to extract longer-term benefits if the operation is backed by policy. 

 'The key question is whether this is a prelude to interest rate changes,' said Michael Burke, currency analyst at Citibank in London. If not, he suggested, the dollar will end up right where it started. 

 The exercise, the first intervention by the major central banks since April 5, certainly came as a surprise. 

 Central banks outside the U.S. had previously made it plain they didn't see the dollar's decline as their problem. Although as many as 19 had participated at one stage last year, their presence in later intervention exercises had become conspicuously token. 

 This time round, however, market sources reported a two rounds sharp round of intervention led by the U.S. Federal Reserve and backed by the other countries in the Group of Ten major industrialized nations (G-10). 

 The Central Bank of Ireland confirmed that smaller countries such as itself weren't asked to participate. The group actually consists of eleven countries: the U.S., Japan, Germany, France, Canada, Italy, Britain, the Netherlands, Sweden, Belgium and Switzerland. 

 The total amount of intervention was hard to gauge with estimates for the exercise ranging up to $5 billion. Julian Jessop, an economist at Midland Global Markets, described it as 'very aggressive.'

title: Market Talk Roundup: Riksbank Raises Rate by 25 Basis Points, Krona Drops
text:
Sweden's Riksbank raised the policy rate by 25 basis points to 3.75% and signaled the need to increase rates further. Some had anticipated a bigger rise, however, and the Swedish krona reaches a record low against the euro later in the day. The Riksbank announced a plan to hedge 25% of its currency reserves, which analysts consider will be insufficient to stop the krona's weakening. The following is a selection of analyst comments.

Riksbank Stresses Hedging Plan Isn't Currency Intervention

1350 GMT - In a surprise move, the Riksbank said it is considering hedging part of its FX reserves to reduce financial risks, but governor Erik Thedeen repeatedly stated in Thursday's press conference that the measure was not to be seen as FX intervention, SEB's Sweden chief strategist Olle Holmgren says in a note. "Considering that the measure was presented at the same time as the rate decision which states that a weaker SEK is the main upside risk for inflation...it seems probable that the Riksbank hopes that the currency hedging will support the krona." EUR/SEK dropped back after the initial run higher this morning, but has headed higher again since Thedeen's comments, SEB says. (dominic.chopping@wsj.com)

Swedish Krona Falls to Record Low Vs Euro as Rate Outlook Looks Uncertain

1327 GMT - The Swedish krona falls to a record low against the euro, according to FactSet, extending losses after the Riksbank earlier hiked interest rates by 25 basis points to 3.75%, when some had anticipated a bigger 50bp increase. The Riksbank faces similar challenges to other central banks but they are "more extreme," leaving substantial uncertainty about the future path of monetary policy, HSBC global economist James Pomeroy says in a note. "Inflation is still well-above its target, the currency remains weak, and the economy is hardly growing in aggregate, with consumer spending falling sharply in recent quarters." HSBC expects data will justify a pause in rate rises in September. EUR/SEK hits a high of 11.8437, FactSet data show. (jessica.fleetham@wsj.com)

Riksbank's Higher Rate Path Addresses Continued Inflation Risks

1125 GMT - The Riksbank stuck to its initial plan of raising its policy rate by 25 basis points but responded to the increased upside risk in inflation by raising the rate path by an additional 20 basis points, which was more than expected, DNB Markets economist Oddmund Berg says in a note. The new rate path peaks at 4.05%, implying another 25 basis points hike later this year and the probability of a final quarter-percentage point hike thereafter. "In our view, the increase [in rate path] is a direct result of international rates rising far more than expected in April and the upside risk to inflation if the SEK continues to weaken." (dominic.chopping@wsj.com)

Riksbank Guidance Looks on the Hawkish Side

1000 GMT - The Riksbank's 25 basis points rate increase to 3.75% was widely expected, but its forward guidance is somewhat more hawkish than expected, Swedbank analysts say in a note. The Riksbank now signals at least one more hike this year, and Swedbank expects 25 basis points in September and November, to a terminal rate of 4.25%. "We continue to view inflationary risks as tilted to the upside, not least due to the record weak SEK. That, coupled with surprisingly hawkish decisions from other central bank recently, is likely to keep the Riksbank in hiking mode for longer." The resilient Swedish economy also makes it easier for the Riksbank to steer monetary policy toward further tightening, Swedbank says. (dominic.chopping@wsj.com)

Riksbank's Currency Hedging Plan Unlikely to Halt Krona's Fall

0930 GMT - The Riksbank's decision to hedge 25% of its SEK400 billion currency reserves will render a positive flow of up to SEK100 billion, which looks a modest amount and is unlikely to stop the trend of the Swedish krona falling, SEB chief strategist Carl Hammer says in a note. "However it is a sign that the weakened exchange rate is pressuring Riksbank and more measures could be implemented should we approach 12.00 in EUR/SEK." EUR/SEK last trades at 11.745, having briefly jupmed to a high of 11.8289 after the Riksbank raised its policy rate by 25 basis points. (dominic.chopping@wsj.com)

Riksbank's 25Bps Rate Rise Disappointed, Weakening The Krona

0918 GMT - The Swedish krona weakened following the Riksbank's rate decision as some had hoped for a larger 50 basis points rate hike rather than the 25 basis points that was delivered, Handelsbanken senior economist Johan Lof says in a note. A practically unanimous economist consensus ahead of Thursday's decision saw the Riksbank raising its key policy rate by 25 basis points, and that was the main scenario among market participants as well, he says. The quantitative tightening acceleration was also widely anticipated. "However, markets were pricing a non-trivial probability for an ultra-hawkish 50 basis points hike surprise, so despite the main scenario materialising, market interest rates declined and the krona weakened on impact."(dominic.chopping@wsj.com)

Riksbank Shows Hawkish Face With Rate Rise, Higher Path

0832 GMT - The Riksbank has shown its hawkish face by raising the policy rate 25 basis points to 3.75% and lifting the rate path by a further 30 basis points to peak at 4.05%, clearly outstripping its April forward guidance, Handelsbanken senior economist Johan Lof says in a note. Adding to the hawkish tilt today is the decision to accelerate the reduction of asset holdings. Despite the more restrictive policy, the Riksbank revised its GDP forecast up, its unemployment forecast down and its CPIF excluding energy forecast up. "All told, that signals an increased awareness of a deeper entrenched inflation problem." Handelsbanken still sees two more 25 basis-point rate rises, in September and November, before cautious rate cuts begin next summer. (dominic.chopping@wsj.com)

Swedish Krona Falls to Multi-Year Low Vs Euro After Riksbank Raises Rates by 25Bps

0754 GMT - The Swedish krona falls to its weakest level in more than a decade after the Riksbank raised its policy rate by 25 basis points to 3.75%, disappointing some in the market who had anticipated a bigger 50bp rise. The falls come even as the Riksbank said rates would rise at least once more this year and opted to increase the pace of government-bond sales from September. The central bank separately announced it was considering hedging around a quarter of its foreign-exchange reserves. EUR/SEK rises to a peak of 11.8289 after the decision, its highest since 2009, according to FactSet, from around 11.7538 beforehand. (jessica.fleetham@wsj.com)

(END) Dow Jones Newswires

title: Riksbank Stresses Hedging Plan Isn't  Currency Intervention  -- Market Talk
text:
0950 ET - In a surprise move, the Riksbank said it is considering hedging part of its FX reserves to reduce financial risks, but governor Erik Thedeen repeatedly stated in Thursday's press conference that the measure was not to be seen as FX intervention, SEB's Sweden chief strategist Olle Holmgren says in a note. "Considering that the measure was presented at the same time as the rate decision which states that a weaker SEK is the main upside risk for inflation...it seems probable that the Riksbank hopes that the currency hedging will support the krona." EUR/SEK dropped back after the initial run higher this morning, but has headed higher again since Thedeen's comments, SEB says. (dominic.chopping@wsj.com)

0942 ET - The rise in Germany's services inflation--to 5.3% in June from 4.5% in May--could spook some European Central Bank policymakers, but they needn't worry, Pantheon Macroeconomics' chief eurozone economist Claus Vistesen says in a note. Base effects in transport services--owing to the anniversary of government rail-fare subsidies--have been well flagged, he says. Indeed, the separate regional CPIs clearly suggest that the jump in services inflation was driven by a jump in the transport services component, Vistesen says. Core inflation will remain elevated due to base effects in transport until August, but then there will likely be a big drop in September as underlying disinflation in goods and services hit the data more meaningfully, he adds. (edward.frankl@wsj.com)

0936 ET - Yield has returned to higher-quality, liquid segments of European fixed-income markets through a combination of higher government bond yields and wider credit spreads, Allspring's fixed-income team says. "We think this presents an opportunity for European and global bond investors to return to euro-denominated credit after many years of sourcing yield globally," Henrietta Pacquement, senior portfolio manager and head of global fixed income and Martijn de Vree, head of fixed income solutions in global fixed income, say. The size of European credit markets offers significant diversification opportunities as well, they say, adding that European investment-grade debt yields about 4%, and yields rise close to 6% when hedged back to the U.S. dollar. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0936 ET - Dockworkers at Canada's western ports of Vancouver and Prince Rupert warn of a three-day strike action starting Saturday over a salary increase impasse with employers. Unions and the British Columbia Maritime Employers Association have been trying to reach a new annual contract since the last contract expired in March. The strike will mostly affect boxships as tankers and other vessels will be allowed to dock. Vancouver and Prince Rupert are Canada's largest and third largest box ports, respectively, and also serve as big gateways for US cargo. (costas.paris@wsj.com)

0933 ET - German inflation figures for June, which were stronger than expected, won't change the European Central Bank's hawkish resolve in its tightening cycle, Franziska Palmas, senior Europe economist at Capital Economics, says in a note. The CPI increased mainly on base effects, with core inflation ticking up entirely due to a jump in services inflation to 5.3% from 4.5%, reflecting the anniversary of the introduction of the EUR9 transport ticket, she says. But even if core inflation edges down in other countries, ECB officials are concerned that the tight labor market will slow the return of the core to target, Palmas says. "Only substantial and repeated falls in core and particularly services inflation would ease those worries," she adds. (edward.frankl@wsj.com)

0928 ET - The US median home listing price slipped 0.9% annually in June, posting the first yearly decline since 2017, Realtor.com says. At the same time, while home shoppers had more homes to choose from this month, improvement stalled as the active inventory growth rate slowed for the fourth month in a row, 7.1%, and came in well below May's 21.5% rate. Price gains have been weakening since last summer as rising mortgage rates have added to ongoing affordability challenges and further cooled buyer demand. Realtor.com says its revised 2023 outlook expects only a modest drop in home prices of 0.6% for the year. (chris.wack@wsj.com)

0928 ET - Higher yields have boosted returns in many bond portfolios year to date, helping investors weather economic uncertainties that continue to unfold around the world, Allspring's fixed income team says in its mid-year outlook. Inflation remains high in both Europe and the U.K., and core inflation in the U.S. remains sticky, it says, adding that this is keeping central banks in inflation-fighting mode. "However, an inflection point may have been reached in the first half of 2023, when central banks had to begin dealing with challenges beyond fighting inflation as global growth slowed and cracks appeared in the financial system," it says. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0927 ET - The Swedish krona falls to a record low against the euro, according to FactSet, extending losses after the Riksbank earlier hiked interest rates by 25 basis points to 3.75%, when some had anticipated a bigger 50bp increase. The Riksbank faces similar challenges to other central banks but they are "more extreme," leaving substantial uncertainty about the future path of monetary policy, HSBC global economist James Pomeroy says in a note. "Inflation is still well-above its target, the currency remains weak, and the economy is hardly growing in aggregate, with consumer spending falling sharply in recent quarters." HSBC expects data will justify a pause in rate rises in September. EUR/SEK hits a high of 11.8437, FactSet data show. (jessica.fleetham@wsj.com)

0925 ET - The tone of the Brazilian central bank's quarterly inflation report was consistent with the start of a cycle of rate cuts, probably as soon as the next monetary policy meeting in August, says Goldman Sachs economist Alberto Ramos in a research note. The bank also raised its forecast for economic growth this year to 2.0% from 1.2%, boosted by the improved outlook for industry, especially mining and utilities, and for services, Ramos says. (jeffrey.lewis@wsj.com)

0920 ET - The rise in German inflation in June should only be a temporary pause before consumer prices ease once again, ING's global head of macro Carsten Brzeski says in a note. The rebound to 6.4%, from 6.1% in May, marks end of the disinflationary trend seen over the last six months, but there is evidence the trend could gain stronger momentum after the summer, he says. On-month food prices dropped for the third consecutive month, while clothing prices fell for the first time since January--a tentative sign of weaker demand and price discounts, Brzeski says. "With still lower-than-expected energy prices, dropping food prices and fading pipeline price pressures in both services and manufacturing, German inflation could come down faster than the ECB expects," he adds. (edward.frankl@wsj.com)

0913 ET - Today's fall in weekly jobless claims "is more likely noise than signal," Pantheon's Ian Shepherdson says in a note about today's data showing a decline to 239K from 265K. "We have no specific explanation for this sudden dip, after three straight weeks in a narrow range from 262K to 265K, but observations for individual weeks always have to be viewed with skepticism, especially when they move against the established trend in claims and other data," Shepherdson says. He adds that, considering seasonal factors, "a modest net dip in claims over the next few weeks is a reasonable bet, even as the underlying trend continues to rise." (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

0910 ET - Consumer spending grew at a 4.2% annual rate in 1Q, the fastest pace since mid-2021, when the economy was rebounding from pandemic lockdowns. Stronger consumer spending was a key driver behind the upward revision to 1Q GDP growth. Consumers splashed out on long-lasting goods in the first three months of the year, despite higher interest rates. Consumer spending on durables rose at a 16.3% annual rate. Their spending on services, which includes dining out and traveling, also notched a solid annual gain of 3.2% in 1Q. (sarah.chaney@wsj.com)

title: Swedish c.bank's Jansson says  currency intervention  would be last resort
text:
STOCKHOLM, May 29 (Reuters) - Sweden's weak currency is a problem but a currency intervention would be a last resort, central bank Deputy Governor Per Jansson said on Monday.

"We have chosen a regime with an inflation target and free-floating currency, those are for me the rules of the game," Jansson told reporters.

"I don't think it is a measure we should take in the kind of system we have. There are also significant questions over the effectiveness of intervention. It can be very expensive for very small effects." (Reporting by Simon Johnson, Editing by Johan Ahlander)

title: Sweden's Riksbank says 'jump', the crown says 'no'
text:
LONDON, May 3 (Reuters) -

Sweden's central bank has tried and failed to talk up its currency and is running out of room to raise rates, leaving the crown languishing around its weakest in 14 years against the euro and undermining its efforts to control inflation.

It's not going to get much better any time soon. Markets are pricing for more rate hikes from the European Central Bank and others, which are hard for the Riksbank to match due to issues in the housing sector.

There is talk about possible official intervention in foreign exchange markets to support the crown, though analysts think it unlikely the Riksbank would resort to this tool in the near term, partly because of its limited reserves.

"We believe in, and want to have, a stronger crown," Riksbank Governor Erik Thedeen told reporters last Wednesday after the bank announced a half-point rate hike to 3.50%.

"If that doesn't happen over time, it could have significance for monetary policy because a weaker crown could lead to higher inflation," he said.

Markets, however, were not listening. The crown weakened as much as 1% that day.

More broadly it has lost 14% in value against both the euro and the dollar since late 2021. In recent months, it has held up better against the dollar, but is trading around its weakest since 2008 against the euro.

The problem, analysts say is markets expect more interest rate rises from the ECB, while the Riksbank last week hinted it was nearly done with tightening and two rate-setters voted for a 25 basis point rate increase.

Kenneth Broux, senior FX and rates strategist at Societe Generale said this "dovish dissent" would mean "more weakness against the euro, as the rate differential moved in the euro's favour".

Traders currently expect 75 basis points more of tightening from the ECB.

Expectations for higher official interest rates typically boost money market and government bond yields, attracting investor cash to a country, which boosts the currency.

The gap between key parts of the Swedish and euro zone rate curves narrowed sharply in 2022 and turned in the euro's favour at the start of this year.

TOUGH SPOT

The weakening crown is a problem for Sweden. It makes imported goods more expensive, thereby adding to inflation, which is already running at 8.9% year-on-year when volatile energy prices are excluded.

"The krona is not the major factor for elevated inflation, but it does play an important role and obviously it would be beneficial to have a strong exchange rate," said Carl Hammer, chief strategist at SEB, using the currency's Swedish name.

Hiking rates further would typically support a country's currency, but it's difficult in Sweden because rate rises have already brought long-standing problems with the housing sector to the fore.

The Riksbank expects house prices to bottom out in early 2024 after falling around 19% from a peak in early 2022.

"It's difficult for the Riksbank to be that hawkish," said Jan von Gerich, chief analyst at Nordea.

"They have an inflation problem, but they also have a housing market that's already in a weak state, and an economy that is coming down."

Households in Sweden are more sensitive to rates than those elsewhere, as around 60% of mortgages are on floating rates.

That leaves the central bank exploring other options to boost the crown.

"I think they will only hike, at the max, one more time. But I think they then increase (quantitative tightening) and then if that doesn't really help, definitely there will be some sort of verbal intervention on the table," said SEB's Hammer.

He said the Riksbank directly intervening in markets seemed a way away.

Such interventions are rate. Sweden bought crowns in 2001 to strengthen the currency, and sold it in 2021 to replace the borrowed part of its foreign exchange reserve.

JPMorgan analysts said the Riksbank's reserves make up less than two days’ worth of daily market volume in dollar/crown and euro/crown trading, potentially limiting the effectiveness of intervention.

Nonetheless, SocGen's Broux said intervention was "on his radar" as he'd been getting client questions about it.

He said the 11.50 crown-per euro level could be one to watch. It is currently at 11.29.

(Reporting by Alun John and Harry Robertson; Editing by Toby Chopra)

title: Sweden 's Riksbank Decides Against Extending Mandate for Rapid  Currency Interventions  -- Market Talk
text:
1013 GMT - The Riksbank 's Executive Board did not extend a mandate for rapid FX interventions that expired Tuesday. The decision indicates a further move away from a focus on the krona, and decreasing concern of rapid appreciation, according to Handelsbanken strategist Claes Mahlen. Worries about a fierce appreciation of the Swedish currency have receded in view of the krona's rapid decline in the past few weeks. The krona, however, strengthened earlier Wednesday as the Riksbank confirmed its intention to lift the key rate in the second half of the year. ( nina.adam@wsj.com, @Nina_Adam_)

0953 GMT - Lower-than-expected inflation data in the U.K. isn't enough to push the pound lower as investors remain focused on uncertainty surrounding Brexit. January's year-on-year consumer price index fell below Bank of England 's 2.0% target for the first time in two years to 1.8% from 2.1% in December. A WSJ poll had forecast a smaller fall to 1.9%. Core CPI remained steady and as expected at 1.9%. The pound is around the same level is was before the release, last down 0.1% at $1.2889. EUR/GBP is up 0.1% at 0.8787. On Monday, the U.K. gross domestic product also came in weaker than expected, which sent the pound lower. (olga.cotaga@wsj.com)

0942 GMT - Inflation data is likely to have dropped in the U.S. due to cheaper oil prices, which should keep EUR/USD "range-locked," says Kit Juckes, macro strategist at Societe Generale . The euro dipped below $1.13 at the beginning of the week as the dollar strengthened slightly, but is now back in the range it had been earlier--between 1.13 and 1.15--and is last flat at $1.1323. The January headline U.S. consumer price index is expected to fall to 1.5% year-on-year from 1.9% a month ago, according to a WSJ poll. Core CPI is expected to fall to 2.1% from 2.2%. (olga.cotaga@wsj.com)

0932 GMT - German two-year bonds, or Schatz, look a logical alternative, at least in the short term, to expensive 10-year Bunds, which it's time to cash in on, DZ Bank analyst Daniel Lenz says. Ten-year Bund yields currently trade at a yield of 0.125%, according to Tradeweb , having recently touched 0.08%, the lowest level since 2016. The two-year Schatz yield trades at -0.57%, according to Tradeweb . The 10-year Bund yield fall is mainly attributable to the deteriorating economic environment in Germany and the eurozone, Mr. Lenz says, adding that Schatz yields haven't replicated this movement. "Quite the opposite," he says, adding that Schatz yields have risen about four bps over the same period. (emese.bartha@wsj.com; @EmeseBartha)

0930 GMT - The Riksbank won't extend the mandate to quickly intervene in FX markets to counteract rapid krona strengthening, as the krona has weakened since December and was 3% off the Riksbank 's forecast ahead of Wednesday's meeting, says Claes Mahlen at Handelsbanken. "This indicates a further move away from the focus on the krona and less worries of fast appreciation." The Riksbank left policy rates and the rate path unchanged, but revised growth forecasts slightly lower. The central bank still sees the next 25 basis point rate increase in October, but the market prices this in April 2020. Handelsbanken expects the Riksbank to carry out the signaled hike in October, with the repo rate staying at zero throughout 2020. (dominic.chopping@wsj.com)

0904 GMT - The Riksbank has acknowledged subdued economic growth in Sweden, but reiterated it is going to increase interest rates in the second half of 2019, pushing the Swedish krona higher. EUR/SEK falls to one-week low of 10.4394 from 10.4909 before the central bank decision to keep repo rate unchanged at minus 0.25%. The central bank also said that "economic activity is still strong" in Sweden and that the "conditions for inflation to remain close to 2% in the coming years have not changed to any great extent." (olga.cotaga@wsj.com)

0859 GMT - Italy's 10-year government bond, or BTP, appears to be eliciting buyers at yields around 3%, says Natixis rates strategist Jean-Christophe Machado. However, when the yield spread over Bunds falls to 250 basis points, "caution is in order," Mr. Machado says. Italy's 10-year benchmark BTP trades at a yield of 2.852%, while the 10-year BTP-Bund spread is 272 basis points, according to Tradeweb . (emese.bartha@wsj.com; @EmeseBartha)

0850 GMT - The greenback has edged through support in Asia trading in the S$1.3560 area, and whether that holds could depend on Friday's Singapore GDP revision. If data show the city-state's economy is holding steady, it may drag the pair closer to its next support level of S$1.3450. Resistance remains near its 50-day moving average of around S$1.3600. The greenback is down 0.1% today. (gaurav.raghuvanshi@wsj.com)

0836 GMT - The cost of three-month sterling options--which help investors protect themselves against large moves in the pound--has risen slightly, but it is still much lower than it was during mid-December last year. This suggests investors are now less worried about a disorderly Brexit. The cost of one-month sterling options has gone down. Still, companies and fund managers are more worried now than they were same time a year ago, given that the cost of three-month options has increased since January 2018. The U.K. parliament is due to vote on the Brexit withdrawal deal again on Thursday. The current Brexit deadline is March 29. (olga.cotaga@wsj.com)

0830 GMT - Societe Generale expects U.K.'s consumer price index inflation--data which will be released at 0930 GMT--to fall from 2.1% to the inflation target at 2%, exactly two years since the target was last reached. It expects core CPI to stay at 1.9% and the commodity part of the CPI basket to fall. By Camilla Knudsen

OSLO, July 5 (Reuters) - The currencies of Sweden and Norway are set to rise in value against the euro over the next 12 months, but will see short-term weakness against the U.S. dollar following the Brexit vote, a Reuters poll found on Tuesday.

The Swedish economy, among Europe's fastest growing, expanded by 4.2 percent year-on-year in the first quarter and continues to benefit from ultra-loose monetary policies that analysts say will be maintained for the time being.

Economists participating in the poll predicted on average that the Swedish crown would rise by almost two percent against the euro in the next three months and by about 4.5 percent to 9.00 in a year's time.

"We still expect fairly strong growth in Sweden, even if we've cut forecasts somewhat following the Brexit vote," Handelsbanken currency strategist Nils Kristian Knudsen said.

"Swedish inflation seems set to rise in the second half of 2016, and we believe the crown will respond positively to that. It's a natural reaction," he added.

Meanwhile, neighbouring Norway is expected to see a moderate economic recovery in 2017 following a slump triggered by the sharp fall in the price of crude oil, the main export.

The Norwegian central bank in March slashed its key policy rate to a record low of 0.5 percent and said in June it would likely cut it again later this year to boost growth and lift the outlook for inflation.

Economists predicted the Norwegian crown would rise by three percent against the euro by the summer of 2017 as the economy gradually recovers.

"We see positive signs in economic data and believe the worst is behind us for the Norwegian economy, and that the growth momentum picks up in the second half of the year," SEB Norway chief strategist Erica Blomgren said.

The Norwegian and Swedish crowns are expected to weaken against the dollar in the next three months though, along with a general weakening of the euro, as Britain's vote to leave the European Union has triggered uncertainty among investors.

Both the Riksbank and Norges Bank have emphasised a need for currency weakness to keep inflation up and help facilitate growth, and in the case of Sweden the central bank even authorised its governor to intervene in the market if necessary.

On a 12-month basis, however, both the Swedish and Norwegian crowns are expected to regain some ground versus the dollar, the poll showed.

title: In Global Fight Over  Currencies , Sweden Weighs Move
text:
(FROM THE WALL STREET JOURNAL 2/5/16) 
   By Charles Duxbury 

STOCKHOLM -- A year after cutting its main interest rate below zero percent for the first time ever, the board of Sweden's central bank is considering further bold moves to keep a buoyant national currency in check and jolt desperately moribund inflation.

As the central bank prepares to announce policy decisions on Feb. 11, even lower interest rates, an extension of a bond-buying program and direct currency-market interventions are on the table, said officials at Sweden's Riksbank.

"We have become seasoned," long-serving Riksbank Deputy Gov. Per Jansson said in an interview. "Things which once made us say 'oh my God' don't seem that dramatic anymore."

Sweden is a small-scale but stark illustration of how many central banks, with a mandate to help tiny but steady inflation percolate through their economies, are wrestling with their currencies.

With the inflow of cheap commodity and energy pushing down price indexes, some central banks have become focused on taking inflation from one another by lowering the value of their national currencies. A weaker currency makes goods coming intothe country more expensive, raising domestic prices.

The Riksbank seized the initiative a year ago when it cut its main rate to minus-0.1%. Since then, its advantage has been checked by sub-zero rate moves by the European Central Bank and, as recently as last week, the Bank of Japan.

Robert Bergqvist, an economist at Stockholm-based Skandinaviska Enskilda Banken AB and a former central-bank official, is concerned this tit-for-tat approach to monetary policy won't be effective. He fears it can at best deliver short-term benefits for growth and inflation but little to address broader challenges, like high public debt or an aging population, which might be driving price growth lower globally.

"This kind of currency war will not benefit anyone," Mr. Bergqvist said.

Central banks have used rate setting to guide their currencies to a desired level in the past. This is the first time so many countries are burrowing through the underlands of monetary policy. In addition to Sweden, the eurozone and Japan, Denmark and Switzerland also have adopted negative interest rates.

Sweden now boasts a benchmark interest rate of minus-0.35% and a deposit rate of minus-1.1%, meaning that the Riksbank is effectively charging banks willing to hold certain types of reserves with the central bank. The policy is designed to encourage banks to lend instead of sitting on cash and to dissuade foreign investors from holding a nation's currency.

The trouble is Sweden's economy is growing at a healthy pace of about 3% a year and is in no particular need of the stimulus provided by negative rates.

Riksbank policy makers said they are aware that housing prices have risen close to 20% in some parts of Sweden over the past year and that their ultra-accommodating policy risks causing bubbles in real estate and other assets. But if they do too little, expected further easing from the ECB next month could send the Swedish currency soaring against the euro. "There is scope to do more," Mr. Jansson said.

The Riksbank found itself at a similar juncture last year. The first move below a zero-percent rate had provided a brief respite. After a few weeks, however, the krona was again rising against the euro, endangering Sweden's exporters by making their goods pricier, while cheaper imports risked sapping the central bank's efforts to rekindle inflation.

Between mid-February and mid-March a fall in the euro from 9.60 Swedish kronor to 9.10 had Mr. Jansson and his colleagues scrambling to react.

On March 18, the Riksbank rushed into an unscheduled policy conclave and decided to go deeper into negative territory, cutting its main rate to minus-0.25% from minus-0.15%.

"It was clear that if that appreciation had continued, we would have been in big trouble," Mr. Jansson said.

Since then, the bank has sanctioned another rate cut and set a target to buy as much as 35% of Sweden's government debt from commercial banks. That is done with newly minted money, again to stimulate the economy by boosting lending.

The inflation target is a cornerstone of the small open Swedish economy, the Riksbank said. Introduced in New Zealand in 1990, the strategy guides wage setting and helps growth by dissuading citizens from saving in the hope of cheaper prices in the future.

Despite its expansive policy, the Riksbank's inflation score card has disappointed and it hasn't hit its 2% target for four years. A year ago, the bank said inflation would hit the target this year, but by year-end its 2016 forecast had been cut to 1.3%. The annual inflation rate in December was 0.1%. To regain leverage, the Riksbank said late last year it was considering intervening in the currency market directly, something it hasn't done in a decade and a half. The policy would involve selling kronor to push down their value.

On Jan. 4, the Riksbank board held an unscheduled meeting and said it was in a position to act anytime. "The upturn in inflation still depends to a large extent on the weak krona," the board said after the meeting.

title: RPT-Struggling to raise inflation,  Sweden  edges towards  currency intervention
text:
(Repeats Friday item)

* Crown strengthening on strong domestic economy, loose ECB policy

* Board gave governor power to intervene in fx market this week

* Rate setters split on intervention decision

By Daniel Dickson and Oskar von Bahr

STOCKHOLM, Jan 8 (Reuters) - Sweden's central bank is close to making its first foreign exchange intervention in 15 years in a desperate attempt to push up inflation, but critics say any effort to weaken the crown is likely to be futile.

The Riksbank has struggled to combat a largely strengthening currency despite cutting interest rates to record negative lows, due to a booming economy and loose monetary policy in much of the outside world.

With its monetary tools to ward off deflation dwindling, the Riksbank board gave Governor Stefan Ingves powers earlier this week to intervene immediately in the currency market. Minutes published on Friday of a meeting last month suggested that some policymakers believe intervention is the right way to go.

"Several members ... noted that if the exchange rate appreciated too rapidly, currency interventions could be necessary," said the minutes of the rate-setting meeting held in mid-December.

The ultra-low interest rates helped the economy to grow 3.9 percent year-on-year in the third quarter, the third highest rate in the European Union. Data on Friday showed industrial production was up 6 percent in November from a year earlier.

But with the main lending rate at -0.35 percent and the Riksbank pumping money into the economy by buying bonds, it faces a quandary. The loose monetary policy is failing to raise inflation but encouraging a rise in house prices and household debt, which per capita is one of the highest in Europe. Many people also fear a housing bubble.

"The tool box is getting empty," said Nordea analyst Torbjorn Isaksson.

That leaves currency intervention to weaken the currency in the hope of pushing inflation towards the Riksbank's target by raising the cost of imported goods and services. Analysts believe the Riksbank could start selling crowns at somewhere between 9.00 to 9.15 to the euro versus 9.26 on Friday.

TARGET OBSESSION

Critics say the bank's obsession with its 2 percent target is unrealistic. But the board does not dare to wait for the strong domestic economy to push up inflation, wary of past policy mistakes that undermined its credibility.

The Riksbank raised rates fast in 2010 and 2011, worried about the housing bubble that was already inflating, even though the global economy had yet to recover from the 2008 financial crisis. Nobel Laureate Paul Krugman called the policy "sadomonetarist" while U.S. Federal Reserve chief Janet Yellen held up premature Swedish rate increases as a mistake to avoid.

Former Bank of England governor Mervyn King and U.S. economist Professor Marvin Goodfriend are due this month to present a post mortem report on the last few years of Swedish monetary policy, including the viability of the inflation target.

Consumer prices have been flat or falling for most of the last three years, and a meagre pick up toward the end of last year has stalled, largely due to the stronger crown. CPI rose by 0.1 pct in the year to November.

FIGHTING AGAINST GRAVITY

Many people think that if the Riksbank resorts to currency intervention, it will be unable to beat the market. "The crown is in our opinion - and according to the Riksbank - undervalued so they are fighting against gravity," Nordea's Isaksson said.

The problems with currency intervention were highlighted only last year when the Swiss central bank was forced to scrap its cap on the Swiss franc versus the euro.

In a sign of a split within the Riksbank, Deputy Governor Martin Floden entered a reservation against the board's decision to give Ingves the powers to intervene immediately.

On its trade-weighted index, the crown has strengthened 5.8 percent since April and is 2.9 percent stronger since the day before the Riksbank cut rates at an unscheduled meeting in March.

Threats of currency intervention have caused the crown to weaken from its strongest levels in December, but the index is still stronger than the Riksbank's latest forecast, at 109.06 versus 110.7 seen around now.

A Reuters poll on Thursday showed that despite the prospects of currency intervention, market strategists expect the crown to reach 9.00 by the end of the year.

Many believe currency intervention will be backed by other policy measures such as further rate cuts and more bond buying.

In Friday's minutes, Floden advocated further rate cuts. However, critics says they cannot be cut infinitely below zero and market participants are already complaining of low liquidity even though the Riksbank has yet to complete purchases of more than 30 percent of outstanding government bonds.

The last time the Riksbankintervened in the currency market was in 2001. At that time, the problem was the opposite: a weakening Swedish crown meant there was a risk of higher inflation than the Riksbank's 2 percent target.

A 2006 study published by the Riksbank itself showed that interventions had been of little value, also after a currency peg that the bank upheld at tremendous costs, including a 500 percent policy rate, until 1992, was scrapped.

"That the Riksbank alone could resist the whole of the market's flows or its will to affect the crown, I just don't believe in that," said Anders Skoldberg, portfolio manager at the Second Swedish National Pension Fund. * Swedish crown seen stronger vs euro despite intervention threat

By Terje Solsvik and Camilla Knudsen

OSLO, Jan 7 (Reuters) - Sweden's crown currency will probably strengthen against the euro in 2016 despite a plan by the country's central bank to weaken it, and its gains are likely to be accompanied by a rally in the Norwegian crown, according to a Reuters poll.

Sweden's consumer prices have been flat or falling for most of the last three years even though its economy is growing. A meagre pickup in prices towards the end of 2015 seems to have stalled, in part because of the crown's recent strength.

The central bank's board, which has slashed interest rates to a record low of minus 0.35 percent, earlier this week authorised its governor to intervene in the market to push down the crown in a bid to boost inflation.

But market strategists expect the crown, which has risen by about three percent against the euro since September, to gain another three percent in 2016 to reach 9.00 by the end of the year.

"Sweden is now among the top international performers in terms of economic growth, making the crown attractive," DNB Markets economist Camilla Viland said. "We believe the crown will remain so even though the central bank is clearly trying to limit the attraction by threatening to intervene."

DNB also predicted that Sweden's inflation rate will rise in 2016, reducing the need for a weaker currency, Viland said.

NOK TO REBOUND DESPITE OIL INDUSTRY WEAKNESS

The currency of neighbouring Norway has weakened, falling around 13 percent to 9.65 against the euro since May as the price of crude oil, Norway's key export, continues to decline. But it is expected to rise by seven percent during the next 12 months to reach 8.95.

The Norwegian central bank, which itself has forecast a somewhat stronger crown, wants to avoid a surge that could hurt the economy at a vulnerable time and has said it is likely to cut rates in March.

Forecasts varied a great deal for both the Swedish and the Norwegian currencies, reflecting differing views among analysts on factors ranging from global growth and interest rates to the price of oil.

The most bearish predicted that both currencies will weaken by over three percent against the euro by the end of 2016. The most bullish expect rallies of around 11 percent.

title: BREAKINGVIEWS- Sweden  ignores Swiss lesson on  FX intervention
text:
(The author is a Reuters Breakingviews columnist. The opinions expressed are her own.)

By Swaha Pattanaik

LONDON, Jan 5 (Reuters Breakingviews) - History's lessons are often ignored. Sweden may be the latest to do so by threatening to intervene to curb the inflation-dampening strength of its currency, the crown.

The clearest sign that the Nordic nation is ready and willing to act came on Jan. 4 when the central bank, known as the Riksbank, gave its governor, Stefan Ingves, the power to sell crowns for foreign currency if a nascent rise in inflation needed protection. It's easy to see why Ingves, who dismissed the option of intervention in November 2014, may have had a change of heart.

The trade-weighted measure of the crown's value has appreciated about 6.5 percent since August 2015, making imported goods ever cheaper. Hardly helpful for a country where consumer prices have basically flatlined for the past three years.

Monetary policy could always be eased further, but cutting rates from their current record low of minus 0.35 percent carries risks for an economy which the government expects will grow by 3.1 percent this year. In particular, it risks boosting household debt, which has already surpassed 175 percent of disposable income. Focusing on weakening the exchange rate would avoid this danger.

The impact of intervention could be short-lived. A 2006 study published in the Riksbank's working paper series found Swedish currency interventions between 1993 and 2002 did little to reverse, accentuate, or moderate exchange rate moves.

Then there is the more recent example of Switzerland, which spectacularly abandoned attempts to cap its currency almost exactly a year ago after a protracted and dogged fight. Few traders expect the Riksbank to put up as much of a fight as its Swiss peer, whose balance sheet ballooned to around 80 percent of the country's GDP before it capitulated.

None of this may prevent the Riksbank from intervening. Like other central banks, low inflation is forcing it to pull all the levers at its disposal, no matter how useless they are.

"The recent appreciation in the Swedish krona creates risks for the upturn in inflation. If the exchange rate strengthens earlier and more rapidly than forecast, it will be more difficult to push up inflation towards the target," Ingves said.

"The Riksbank is therefore highly prepared to intervene on the exchange market whenever we deem it necessary", he added.

title: IMF Executive Board Concludes 2015 Article IV Consultation with Sweden
text:
Release date - 02122015

On November 30, 2015 the Executive Board of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) concluded the Article IV consultation1 with Sweden.

Sweden's economy is performing well, with real GDP growth of 3.4 percent per year in the first three quarters of 2015, up from 2.3 percent in 2014. Job creation was robust in the first three quarters of 2015, helping bring the unemployment rate down to 7.2 percent in the third quarter. Solid growth of about 3 percent is expected to continue into 2016.

Core inflation (HICP basis) rose to 1.4 percent per year on average in recent months, but remains below the 2 percent target. Since early 2015 the Riksbank has implemented negative interest rates, cutting the repo rate in three steps to -0.35 percent. It is also purchasing 135 billion Swedish Kronor in government bonds in 2015, some 20 percent of the outstanding stock, and further purchases are planned in the first half of 2016.

Migration inflows to Sweden have surged to over 1.5 percent of the population in 2015, with the majority being asylum seekers, and these inflows could remain high. Historical experience is that the employment rates of migrants rise toward the high level of Swedes, but this integration process is lengthy. Unemployment rates among the foreign born, as with the low skilled, are notably higher than the overall unemployment rate.

Housing price inflation has accelerated to 18 percent per year, partly reflecting urban population growth outpacing new housing construction. Mortgage credit growth rose to 8 percent per year in September, lifting household debt to a new high of 176 percent of disposable income, with about 22.5 percent of households with a mortgage having a debt-to-income (DTI) ratio over 500 percent.

Executive Board Assessment2

Executive Directors welcomed Sweden's solid economic growth, which reflects supportive macroeconomic policies and strong domestic demand. Directors noted, however, that Sweden faces major challenges including a sharp rise in migrant inflows, rapidly rising housing prices and elevated household debt, and inflation that remains below target. Directors called for policies to work together to address these intertwined challenges so as to contain medium-term risks to growth.

Directors commended Sweden's humanitarian migration policy and well-developed introduction program for refugees. Yet unemployment rates for the low-skilled and foreign-born are considerably higher than average. Directors therefore stressed the importance of reforms to broaden job creation and facilitate integration. They suggested that entry-level wages and employment protection should not be a barrier to hiring groups with high unemployment, and recommended that the authorities better align training with employer's needs and improve the effectiveness of public job matching services.

Directors endorsed the stimulatory stance of monetary policy to address weak inflation expectations and protect the effectiveness of the inflation target in promoting macroeconomic stability. They supported the Riksbank's readiness to do more, if needed, until core inflation is durably close to target, but considered that the authorities should refrain from foreign exchange intervention except as a last resort given Sweden's strong external position.

Directors agreed that the broadly neutral fiscal stance is appropriate. They considered that additional migration-related expenses should be accommodated in the near term, noting that investments in helping migrants integrate will reduce costs in the medium term and support their contribution to growth. Such expenses should be funded over time as part of achieving the medium-term fiscal target. Directors considered that balancing the central government budget on average over the cycle would be sufficient to safeguard Sweden's fiscal buffers.

Directors highlighted the need for broad-based efforts to rebalance the housing market to protect stability and help sustain growth. To increase housing supply they called for reforms to enable greater competition in residential construction, together with a general phasing out of rent controls, with vulnerable households protected by the housing allowance. Directors also urged phasing out mortgage interest deductibility, raising the limit on capital gains tax deferrals, and expanding subsidies for building affordable rental apartments in areas with jobs to support a soft landing of housing prices, while also aiding labor mobility and migrant integration.

Directors emphasized that the legal framework for macroprudential policies needs to be strengthened to give the FSA access to a range of tools to address risks in a timely and efficient way. They supported the planned adoption of a regulation on the amortization of high loan-to-value mortgages. Directors recommended that Sweden also limit the share of mortgages with high debt-to-income ratios to reduce vulnerabilities associated with further housing price increases.

title: Negative rates merited, but  Sweden  should avoid  FX intervention -IMF
text:
STOCKHOLM, Dec 2 (Reuters) - Sweden's central bank has been right to adopt ultra-loose monetary policy but should not intervene in the currency market to push up prices unless absolutely necessary, the International Monetary Fund said on Wednesday.



Despite growth that is outpacing most of the developed world, benchmark rates in Sweden stand at a record low of minus 0.35 percent to help the central bank boost inflation.



In its annual report on Sweden, the IMF backed the negative rates and "supported the Riksbank's readiness to do more, if needed, until core inflation is durably close to target".



But it said the Riksbank should not intervene in foreign exchange market, "except as a last resort given Sweden's strong external position".



The country has been running a large current account surplus for decades and a devaluation of the crown would make exporters even more competitive.



Negative rates have started to push up consumer prices with  underlying inflation at 1.1 percent on an annual basis in October, but the Riksbank has said it will act again if the upturn is threatened.



With little room to cut rates further or expand its bond purchases, the central bank has said it could consider currencyintervention as a way to weaken the crown currency and push up import prices.



The country faces further challenges in addition to low inflation, the IMF said.



As many as 190,000 asylum seekers are expected to arrive this year and while many will have their claims rejected, the flood is straining short-term resources and will add to long term problems in the labour market, housing and the education system.



The IMF called on authorities to adopt a range of measures, including phasing out mortgage interest tax breaks, to cool down a red-hot housing market. Rent controls should be abolished and reform is needed to boost competition in construction, it said.



Sweden's authorities have been growing increasingly concerned a housing bubble is building, with prices soaring and mortgage debt levels among the highest in Europe.



But measures to address the problems have been delayed.



The IMF said it expected Sweden's economy to grow around 3 percent both this year and next. Growth in the euro zone is expected to be around 1.5 percent this year, according to the OECD.



(Reporting by Simon Johnson; editing by Niklas Pollard)

title: RPT-Sweden risks property bubble as  currency  war intensifies
text:
(Repeats from Sunday, without changes)

* Riksbank steps up efforts to avoid deflation

* Strengthening crown seen as threat

* Monetary loosening could stoke consumer debt

* Key interest rate at -0.25 pct

By Johan Ahlander and Simon Johnson

STOCKHOLM, March 22 (Reuters) - Having twice cut rates into negative territory, Sweden's central bank is locked in a high-stakes currency war with the European Central Bank that could stave off deflation but risks creating another property bubble.

The Riksbank is worried that a strengthening crown, fuelled in part by ECB bond-buying, will reverse a recent upturn in consumer prices and raise the spectre of deflationary damage to Sweden's fast-growing AAA economy.

The moves by Riksbank Governor Stefan Ingves represent a dramatic rethink by a bank that was accused of "sado monetarism" for keeping policy tight after the financial crisis for fear of stoking household debt that is among the highest in Europe at 170 percent of disposable income.

The Riksbank cut its key interest rate by 0.15 percentage points last week, to -0.25 percent, and said it would buy a further 30 billion Swedish crowns ($3.5 billion) of government bonds.

The danger, however, is that the ultra-loose monetary policy could encourage households to take on more debt.

"Our fundamental view is that they have been forced to take this aggressive action because of past mistakes," said James McCann, European economist at Standard Life Investments.

"The risk for them is if they go big on asset purchases it could feed through into bigger credit creation in the housing sector and they would be stoking financial stability risk."

CRIPPLING CRASH

Memories of Sweden's crippling property crash of the early 1990s remain vivid. Though set against a different backdrop -- high inflation was then endemic in Sweden -- a real estate lending boom crippled several banks as loans went bad, necessitating a costly state rescue.

The rest of the decade was spent slowly restocking public finances amid soaring unemployment that even now has yet to return to pre-crisis levels.

Making the Riksbank sweat now is a fall in long-term inflation expectations before wage negotiations for about a third of the country's population are finalised early next year. The deflationary scenario could become self-fulfilling if unions and bosses agree meagre salary increases.

Former finance minister Anders Borg said the Riksbank's slow reaction on low inflation meant it could ill afford a strong crown. Combined with low interest rates, fast economic growth threatens to create asset bubbles, especially in property.

"We must see some of the history coming here. Sweden has now had falling inflation for the past four years ... so it is quite clear we overestimated the inflationary pressures," Borg said, serving to explain why Sweden is taking a looser line than Britain, another European economy with good growth but deflation risks.

QUESTION OF TRUST

Par Magnusson, chief analyst at Nordics RBS, said: "Now inflation expectations are falling, so they are forced to go all in. How do you solve that? By giving a promise to the export industry that you will be weakening the crown ... The message is aimed at the employers: trust us and raise the wages and we will promise to weaken the crown."

The Riksbank's strategy may be working. The crown on Friday traded at around 9.32 to the euro, compared with 9.17 before the central bank's action..

But other small countries, such as Switzerland, have had trouble winning a currency war against the euro, with the ECB pledging to buy 60 billion euros ($64.9 billion) of bonds each month.

"It will be an extremely difficult task," said Robert Bergqvist, chief economist at SEB. "It's a very uneven battle between the ECB and the Riksbank."

If rate cuts fail, Sweden has other tools at its disposal, including currency intervention or increased bond buying. Many traders expect more action if the crown strengthens again.

"I think they can win the war if they increase the size of the asset purchases," said Petr Krpata, currency strategist at ING in London. ($1 = 8.6210 Swedish crowns) ($1 = 0.9242 euros)

(Additional reporting by Johan Sennero; Writing by Alistair Scrutton; Editing by David Goodman)

title: Swedish cbank has not ruled out  currency intervention -Skingsley
text:
STOCKHOLM, March 17 (Reuters) - Sweden's central bank has not ruled out intervening in the currency market as a possible measure to push up inflation, Deputy Governor Cecilia Skingsley said on Tuesday.

"We can make further rate cuts, further bond purchases and also on the list is the possibility of lending to businesses and we have not excluded currency intervention either" Skingsley told reporters on the sidelines of a conference.

She would not give a ranking of the measures available.

Skingsley said a recent pick-up in inflation figures showed that expansive policy was working but that inflation was still too low and that meant that "we are still on high alert to take further measures if we don't think the development is sufficiently favourable".

In February, the Riksbank cut its key interest rate to -0.10 percent and launched a bond buying program to push up prices and restore faith in its 2 percent inflation target.

The Riksbank also said it was ready to act on very short notice with further measures if needed.

text:
NEW YORK, March 6 (Reuters) - Sweden's crown has appreciated sharply since the central bank cut rates and announced a bond-buying programme in mid-February, Deputy Riksbank Governor Per Jansson said on Friday.

"I think we have had now a sharp appreciation," he said.

Jansson told reporters recently a sharp appreciation of the crown would be "game over" in terms of the central bank being able to meet its 2 percent inflation target.

Jansson did not rule out the Riksbank intervening in the currency market.

"It's part of the package. We cannot rule out anything so it's certainly part of the package we've discussed along with other measures, but it's hard to discuss single elements of the package but it's certainly there as a point that's being discussed," he said.

JONKOPING, Sweden, Feb 19 (Reuters) - Currency intervention is still an option for the Swedish central bank but is not reasonable at the Swedish crown's current level, Deputy Riksbank governor Per Jansson told reporters on Thursday.

"Currency intervention is still there as a possibility, but clearly when the crown is weak ... the likelihood that we will use that measure decreases," Jansson said.

"But it depends on the situation and the picture can change if the crown strengthens, we will have a new situation and we will have to think about it again."

At the crown's current level "it is not reasonable that we would do anything", he said.

title: With  currency  war threatening, speculators focus on Swedish crown
text:
LONDON, Feb 5 (Reuters) - Speculators are turning their attention to the Swedish crown, expecting it to weaken as Sweden reacts to the threat of a widening currency war in Europe.

Sweden's Riksbank might open fire as early as next week by cutting interest rates to less than zero and setting the stage for quantitative easing. But if those efforts fall short, analysts say, the central bank may need to intervene directly to weaken the crown.

The European Central Bank's 1.1 trillion-euro quantitative easing programme, announced last month, pushed the euro lower against a host of European currencies. In response, the Swiss National Bank abandoned its cap on the value of the franc and Denmark's central bankintervened in record amounts.

"The Riksbank should intervene and talk the crown down like the Swiss and the Danes. That will have a much bigger impact on the currency than quantitative easing or rate cuts," said Carl Hammer, chief currency strategist at SEB, a leading Nordic bank.

However, the Riksbank has not intervened in the currency market for more than a decade, so it is unlikely to do so immediately.

In the options market, investors are betting on a sustained period of crown weakness. One-month euro/Swedish crown risk reversals -- a gauge of demand for options on a currency rising or falling -- show an increasing bias for crown weakness against the euro.

The pricing partly reflects expectations the central bank will begin a QE programnme of its own. Central bank asset purchases usually weaken a currency by increasing its supply, but the Riksbank is expected to buy only 15 billion to 20 billion crowns (232.75 million euros) a month.

That will be dwarfed by the European Central Bank's 60 billion euros a month, so it is unlikely to be a game changer. [ID:nL6N0V52J6} Indeed, a Reuters poll released on Wednesday forecast the crown would rise to 9.36 crowns per euro in three months from 9.44 now, and to 9.33 in six months.

CURRENCY WARS

Unlike the Swiss and the Danes, Sweden's central bank has a relaxed attitude towards its currency. The last time Sweden intervened was in 2001, when it was trying to support the crown.

"We would not rule out intervention in the FX market later on, but that is probably going to be the last resort," said Susanne Galler, a currency strategist at Jefferies.

Things have changed since 2001, though. At the height of the euro zone crisis in 2012, investors piled into the crown, thanks to Sweden's sound public finances and high credit ratings.

As the crisis ebbed and growth in Sweden weakened, the crown fell. But after the ECB announced its QE programme on Jan. 22, the crown reached a two-month high against the euro. The gains worsened the threat of deflation and bolstered the view that the Riksbank needs to act fast.

The crown's response to unconventional measures will be key to Riksbank efforts to lift inflation back towards its target of 2 percent from -0.3 percent now and whether it finally resorts to intervention.

"If the crown does not depreciate significantly, then QE would probably provide only limited stimulus," Tina Mortensen, economist at Citi.

"And against the likely background of QE and/or rate cuts from the ECB, Danish central bank, Swiss National Bank, Norges Bank and BOJ, a decision to start QE in Sweden may have relatively little effect on the exchange rate." (Reporting by Anirban Nag; Editing by Larry King)

title: Swedish c.bank's Jansson:crown would need to be stronger before  intervention
text:
STOCKHOLM, Nov 18 (Reuters) - Sweden's crown currency would have to appreciate considerably before currency intervention become an option, central bank Deputy Governor Per Jansson said on Tuesday.

"The crown has to appreciate considerably before that's an option," he told reporters.

Jansson also said all option would be on the table if the central bank needed to do more to fight low inflation, including a negative repo rate.

However, he said that there was not a "particularly high probability" of negative interest rates being adopted. (Reporting by Johan Sennero)

title: DJ  Currency  Wars Are Back. Best Be Prepared Says RBS
text:
Talk is building of an all-out currency war as policy makers line up to complain that some countries are gaining an unfair trade advantage by depressing their currencies to improve their competitiveness.

But which countries are most likely to get involved if a currency war breaks out?

In a research note Wednesday, Royal Bank of Scotland says it has some of the answers based on a country's willingness to intervene in FX markets and its capacity to do so, given the structure of its economy.

Among emerging markets, the U.K. bank singles out Malaysia, Thailand, and Chile as three candidates likely to lean against currency appreciation, along with the Czech Republic, a relative "newcomer to currency manipulation."

RBS strategists David Petitcolin and David Simmonds say Sweden, which has traditionally not intervened in markets, could also join the melee.

In contrast, China's willingness to intervene is tempered by the resilience of its exports, while in Brazil exports account for only a small proportion of the overall economy, they say.

That sits oddly with Brazil's relatively aggressive intervention last year. Brazil's finance minister Guido Mantega first coined the phrase "currency wars" in 2010 to describe the global fallout from the monetary policy easing in developed countries.

He accused the U.S. Federal Reserve and other major central banks of flooding financial markets with cash to depress their currencies as investors plowed this cash into emerging markets in search of higher returns.

Brazil and other emerging markets subsequently took steps to stem these pressures.

And more than two years on, the urge to keep currencies in check appears to be returning.

A new government in Japan looks determined to turn the tide on two decades of deflation and the yen has weakened to levels not seen since June 2010. At the same time, the Federal Reserve continues to pump money into the debt-laden U.S. economy.

"For the quantitative easing-leading Japan and U.S., currency competitiveness is not the lead policy obsession," said RBS. "Rather, it's a welcome consequence of the need to loosen financial conditions to reflate domestically."

But what's welcome for some countries is not so welcome for others.

On Wednesday, the Russian central bank's first deputy chairman Alexei Ulyukayev warned that these policies were leading to global imbalances. Meanwhile, Eurogroup head Jean-Claude Juncker spoke late Tuesday of a "dangerously high" euro exchange rate.

Even the Bank Of England, which has a history of not intervening, has railed in recent months against the strength of the pound.

As RBS puts it: "This year could see [the] currency fracas morph into something more internationally combustible: a global currency war."

Focus in the Nordics Thursday will be on third-quarter earnings from Swedish clothing retailer Hennes & Mauritz (HM-B.SK). While the giant fashion retailer published sales already two weeks ago, investors will be keen to know how the company's gross margin and bottom line have fared in the quarter.

Analysts hope lower sourcing costs have raised the margin, but at the same time the company mainly sources in dollars and sells in euros; so the currency development in recent months is likely to have weighed on results. Investors will be interested to learn by just how much.

The general mood for European stocks soured Wednesday and the euro slid to a two week-low against the dollar, as worries about Spain and Greece and the ongoing discord between euro-zone leaders roiled markets. On the macro front, Norges Bank Governor Olsen will give a speech Thursday. According to DNB the strong NOK will contribute towards Norges Bank leaving its policy interest rate unchanged at 1.5% until October 2013. The bank also said that low international forward rates and recurrent waves of financial turmoil also signal an unchanged Norges Bank rate for longer than previously expected.

DNB analyst Kjersti Haugland said that the strong NOK will contribute towards Norges Bank leaving its policy interest rate unchanged at 1.5% until October 2013. NORDIC MARKETS: 

Thursday Swedish clothing retailer Hennes & Mauritz AB reports full earnings for the third quarter at 0600 GMT. The Swedish retailer has already reported third quarter sales, which came in below expectations, due to a rainy summer and unusually warm weather in August in the company's main markets. But investors will closely watch how the company's gross margin has performed in the third quarter, and to what extent a weak euro and continued investments have offset lower sourcing costs.

"Visibility is always low going into H&M results due to the lack of detailed guidance," Societe Generale said in a note.

Aside from that, global events continue to determine sentiment and investors continue to fret over how the euro zone debt crisis will hit Nordic companies. In Greece, workers stage national strikes, and in Spain a call for early elections in the Catalonia region and anti-austerity street protests make Spain's situation look increasingly unstable.


ENERGY: 

Crude-oil futures were slightly higher in Asia trade, recovering some of Wednesday's falls on concerns about Europe, high oil stocks and weakening fuel demand. "From a broader based or macro perspective, we will continue to emphasize a disconnect between WTI crude oil and the equities as the petroleum complex continues to follow the euro lower," energy consulting firm Ritterbusch and Associates said. "We look for the euro zone to continue to be prioritized near term over any risk-on trade that might be implied by a steady stock market." It added that a weaker euro could push Nymex crude below $90/bbl. It also noted that, for the rest of the week, a slew of U.S. economic data releases could support the stock market, but news about the bailout in Spain and Greece will be the main driver of oil prices. November Nymex crude was up 38 cents at $90.36/bbl while Brent was up 34 cents at $110.38/bbl.


NEWS ROUNDUP: 

NORWAY: Norway's seasonally adjusted unemployment rate fell to 3.0% in July from 3.1% the previous month, data from Statistics Norway showed Wednesday. Unemployment in June was revised up to 3.1% from 3.0%, it said. Economists polled by Dow Jones Newswires had forecast an unemployment rate of 3.1% in July.

ESTONIA: Ardo Hansson, the new president of Estonia's central bank, said euro-zone governments may have relied too much on the European Central Bank to fix the region's problems, urging cash-strapped countries to do their part by revising fiscal policy.

"Maybe until now the governments have laid too big hopes on the role of the ECB, but I guess at the moment we all understand that everybody has to participate, especially those countries that are in trouble," Mr. Hansson said.

DENMARK: Niels Bernstein, the Danish central bank governor, said the Danish banking sector is still adapting to the impact of the financial crisis, but will come through it considerably strengthened. Mr. Bernstein said the Danish financial sector will continue to battle bad-loan problems for some time, but new regulations and higher firewalls will help the sector to withstand future crises.

SWEDEN: Swedish consumer confidence dipped again in September in a sign that the debt crisis in Europe is weighing on sentiment even in the region's stronger economies. The closely watched consumer confidence indicator from the National Institute of Economic Research fell to 2.0 from 5.4 in August. This came as a surprise to economists polled by Dow Jones Newswires, who had forecast a rise to 5.7.

SWEDEN: Alfa Laval AB (ALFA.SK), a Swedish maker of heat exchangers, separators, pumps and valves, said it secured an order of 50 million Swedish kronor ($7.62 million) to supply Alfa Laval Aalborg boilers to an offshore oil production vessel in Vietnam.

FINLAND: Fortum Oyj (FUM1V.HE), a Finnish utility, said it has signed a co-operation agreement with Nissan Motor Co. Ltd. (7201.TO) for quick-charging stations in the Nordics. The aim is to create quick-charging infrastructure for electric vehicles to make them a viable option for all car drivers, it said.

SWEDEN: Saab AB (SAAB-B.SK), a Swedish defense company, said it has received a $31 million order from the U.S. army for the company's Carl-Gustaf man-portable weapon system.

FINLAND: Lemminkainen Oyj (LEM1S.HE), a Finnish construction company, said the Finnish competition authorities have approved the sale of its concrete business to Rudus without conditions.

title: Swedish c.bankers say  currency intervention  very unlikely
text:
STOCKHOLM, Sept 18 (Reuters) - Sweden's central bank is very unlikely to intervene in the currency market to steer the level of the Nordic country's record-strong currency, two of the bank's six governors said on Tuesday.

 The Swedish crown hit a 12-year high against the euro in August and despite easing over the last month remains at levels not seen since late 2001, causing problems for some of Sweden's export companies.

 "The way that the crown and the crown movements affect us in our monetary policy decisions is the effect on inflation and resource utilisation," Deputy Riksbank Governor Karolina Ekholm said in a parliamentary hearing.

 Ekholm said should the crown strengthen so much as to risk creating deflation, the central bank would adjust the repo rate to encourage a rise in prices.

 "That the Riksbank would intervene to bring down the level of the crown, that, I think is extremely unlikely."

 Governor Stefan Ingves, giving testimony to parliament alongside Ekholm, said he seconded that comment and noted there was "very little" chance the Riksbank would intervene in the currency market.

 Ingves also noted that the recent strength of the crown currency  was not exceptional in historic terms and was natural in a situation with robust currency account surpluses.
