title: UPDATE 1-Sweden's "Mr Fix It" offers crisis lessons for Europe
text:
(Adds details, background)

STOCKHOLM, Feb 14 (Reuters) - A property bubble, banks near collapse, a currency under pressure and the future of a cushy European social welfare state in question.

This is not Europe 2012 but Sweden 1992. And Bo Lundgren, the fast-talking politician and financial official known as "Mr. Fix It", who then helped rescue Sweden from its worst crisis since the 1930s, says history lessons are being forgotten.

Quick moves over failing banks, including nationalisation and blanket debt guarantees, helped ease a financial crunch. It proved so successful that Lundgren has found himself testifying to the U.S. Congress on the model.

It was also mixed with cautious austerity that Lundgren says avoided the "fiscal trap" facing many European nations in 2012, combined with deep structural reforms and unified political leadership that secured Sweden's economic health for years.

"With luck, and to some extent understanding the situation, we didn't make the mistakes you can see in Europe today ... believing too much in austerity," said Lundgren, who was minister for fiscal and financial affairs from 1991 to 1994 and who now heads Sweden's Debt Office.

From a welfare basket case, Sweden emerged from its crisis as one of Europe's soundest economies - its public debt halving to around 40 percent of GDP since the crisis. It weathered a 2008-09 global crunch in part due to this trauma 20 years ago.

There are major differences - perhaps the most important being Sweden's ability to devalue its currency to boost its export economy - a tool unavailable for countries like Greece.

But Sweden avoided the political conflicts over austerity that Greece now faces and steered clear of the fiscal trap that has led to fears that countries like Spain will be plunged into a spiral of spending cuts, falling revenues and rising debt.

ANOTHER BUBBLE

By 1992, years of deregulation of credit markets had led to a property bubble in Sweden. With house prices rising, people were refinancing their mortgages to renovate, or buying boats to sail at the weekends on Stockholm's archipelago.

Officials paint a picture of a nation at first in denial. Like the United States later, few predicted how much a housing squeeze would spark fires in the rest of the financial system.

"I would get phone calls from Riksbank (central bank) officials and very senior politicians who just did not understand what was happening," said Knut Hallberg, an economist at Swedbank who worked in the finance ministry in the crisis.

When the bubble burst, it sparked a credit crunch.

At one point overnight interest rates rose to 500 percent as the central bank tried to defend a peg of the crown against the German mark. The peg was later abandoned and the crown sank.

The economy contracted by its worst rate since the 1930s. Banks, on average, lost about 20 percent of their balance sheets. Unemployment rose to 12 percent.

Arne Karlsson, CEO of Swedish private equity firm Ratos , said five people he knew committed suicide. He believes any more austerity would have made things even worse.

"We had a very non-Swedish situation at the time," he said. "We had a true depression."

For many, it showed how the Nordic region's biggest economy would be unable to support a cradle-to-grave welfare state that had hit public finance and discouraged productivity and investment. Several small government austerity packages tried to paper over the cracks, but failed.

A TURNAROUND

Realising that this was no ordinary crisis, the government soon extended guarantees to all bank liabilities. Two of Sweden's biggest banks were nationalised, part of government intervention that would cost 4-5 percent of GDP.

It was also a sign of how Sweden rose above party ideology in a crisis. This was no socialist government, but a right of centre coalition -- the same coalition that is in power today.

"As you know I am a market-economy, right-wing politician. But I still believe you can go in and take over the bank for a short while," Prime Minister Fredrik Reinfeldt told Reuters.

"If they want us to cover their losses, we should also be part of the game. If you want our money we will take shares from you," he added. "This is exactly what we learnt in the 1990s. We did it again in 2008-2009."

In 1992, the government even made private banks pay back government consultancy fees.

What's done is done -- and Lundgren says Europe missed an opportunity a year ago in not guaranteeing future loans, and nationalising some failing banks.

He says the more immediate lesson for the Europe of 2012 was Sweden's caution over fiscal austerity. While it was painful - some 5 to 6 percent of GDP - it was spread over several years and combined with structural reforms that would soon help Sweden find lasting long-term growth.

The reforms included a shake up of the tax system which led to lower rates of income tax for workers, but broadened the tax base with the aim of making it fairer and more efficient.

The central bank was also later given its independence and inflation-targetting was introduced.

The country introduced fiscal rules to cap the budget deficit and spending and the pension system was changed to make it more sustainable in the long term.

Sweden was opened up to more competition, particularly with entry to the European Union in 1995.

Nevertheless, ordinary Swedes did suffer in the crisis due to surging unemployment, with the rate never falling back to pre-crisis levels of about 2 percent.

Hans Tson Soderstrom, professor at the Stockholm School of Economics, was invited by the authorities to meet IMF missions who flew in to Stockholm demanding austerity.

"We had shouting matches. The IMF just didn't see the risks of too much austerity," he said. "After a while they didn't invite me back to these meetings."

After the crisis, consumers began to repay debts. The domestic savings ratio was -8 percent of GDP before the crisis, but by 1993 it was plus 12 percent, a shift of a fifth of GDP.

A January report by the McKinsey Global Institute says Sweden's banking measures were critical to kick-start lending. It warned cutting spending too aggressively can slow recovery, as happened in Finland in 1992 amid private debt deleveraging.

"We started out with some kind of rather mild austerity measures," Lundgren said. "Instinctively we understood that you couldn't do so much when you have this phase of the private sector debt consolidation."

"Austerity measures would then only add to the problems we had. You cannot go to markets and say we are doing austerity measures, 'Hey, please lower long-term yields',"

Included in the Swedish austerity moves were cuts in housing subsidies that amounted to 2 percent of GDP and reductions in grants for the unemployed. Energy taxes were indexed.

When Lundgren was forced to raise revenues, he refused to raise tax rates but instead closed loopholes, such as tax deductions.

For Carl Bildt, who was prime minister during the crisis and is now the country's foreign minister, the lesson was using the opportunity to pass structural reforms with a long-term effect.

"Without the devaluation we would have got the same result, but more slowly," he said.

"But it was the structural reforms that led to Sweden's long-term health," he added, referring to polices like abolishing housing subsidies and deregulating telecommunications.

Political unity also helped. The first sentence of the government press release announcing the rescue of the banks made it clear it was an agreement signed with the opposition.

Minority coalition partners and the opposition were generally in accord, despite knowing it was political suicide.

STOCKHOLM (Dow Jones)--Swedish Finance Minister Anders Borg Wednesday said it is vital that agreements are reached on ways to handle struggling banks in Europe, adding that he sees more openness at European Union level to find solutions following the recent meeting of EU finance ministers.

"We have to get these backstops in place--structures for recapitalizing and restructuring banks," Borg told reporters in Stockholm. "What was positive with yesterday's meeting was that there was a greater openness to acting on an EU-level on these questions than previously."

He added that "a solution must be found within a month."

Moving to Sweden's currency, Borg said a worsening of the European debt crisis would weaken the krona, but it has been "a bit more stable than previously" during the market turbulence.

The weakening of the krona during the financial crisis which began in 2008 helped stabilize Sweden's economy, he said.

Borg said the strength of the krona after the recent move by the Swiss National Bank to limit the Swiss franc's strength against the euro had been a concern, but it only lasted a few days.

Pegging the krona to the euro would be the "worst of all worlds," Borg said.

"The advantage of being in the euro zone is that you have access to the European Central Bank's financing and you get security for your banking system. If you just peg the krona you lose the airbag effect of the currency and you don't get the stability of being part of the ECB's system," he said.

title: Swedish Riksbank to publish  intervention  details.
text:
STOCKHOLM, Feb 6 (Reuters) - Sweden's Riksbank, proclaiming greater openness than other central banks, said on Wednesday it will publish regular details of any currency intervention in future, formalising a practice introduced last summer. 

 The Riksbank's intervention policy may become the focus of market scrutiny if Swedes vote in favour of joining Europe's monetary union and their now freely floating crown is linked to the ERM-2 exchange rate grid. 

 Once in ERM-2 the crown would be kept in a tight fluctuation band, if necessary through central bank action. 

 The Riksbank, which dating from the mid-17th century is the world's oldest central bank, said its intervention information policy entailed "much greater transparency" than is common among central banks. 

 "It is important that the bases for all decisions, including those on interventions, are reported in an open and clear manner," it said. 

 The Swedish government has hinted at plans to hold a referendum on euro membership next year. According to a tentative timetable unveiled by Prime Minister Goran Persson last month, the crown might then enter ERM-2 in February 2004. 

 The Riksbank came under fire last summer when it intervened repeatedly, attempting to shore up the then steadily weakening crown. 

 The crown has been floating since the early 1990s and the Riksbank's main monetary policy objective is to keep inflation at on average two percent. Last summer the Riksbank said the softening crown posed a latent threat to its inflation target. 

 "Interventions in the foreign exchange market are primarily a means of signalling and emphasising changes in monetary policy; a process that is necessary to maintain price stability," the Riksbank said on Wednesday. 

Intervention might be used selectively for other economic policy purposes as well, including "to influence the exchange rate or to promote the efficient functioning of the foreign exchange market," it said. 

 FIVE PERCENT UPSIDE 

 According to the consensus forecast in a recent Reuters poll of economists, the Swedish unit would enter ERM-2 at a central parity rate of 8.70 crowns per euro, or over five percent stronger than its present level around 9.20 . 

 "Interventions will continue to be used with restraint," the Riksbank said, adding its monetary policy-making board had decided at a meeting on January 31 that two separate decisions would be taken in conjunction with any foreign exchange intervention. 

 One would be "an outline of the motives behind interventions", the other "a nominal intervention mandate", the latter spelling out how much of the bank's foreign exchange reserves could be committed in an intervention, Riksbank board adviser Anders Borg told Reuters. 

 The main elements in the outline of motives will normally be published in a press release, the bank said. 

 Borg said the press release would be published in connection with the intervention but there was no fixed procedure determining when such a press release would be issued. 

 "The considerations with regard to motives for interventions will be reported in separate minutes, which will normally be published with some time lag," the Riksbank said. 

 Decisions on the intervention mandate, which would also usually include the time period during which the interventions could be made, would be recorded in separate minutes. These would not be published if that would be counter-productive, it said.

title: Riksbank says June  interventions  helped crown, CPI.
text:
STOCKHOLM, Nov 30 (Reuters) - Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, said on Friday its crown purchases in June had helped break the currency's steep fall and contributed to lowering inflation expectations. 

 In minutes of board meetings held on June 14 and July 5, released on Friday, the central bank said the interventions, in which it bought a total of 12 billion Swedish crowns ($1.13 billion), were necessary to send a signal to the market that it was taking its inflation target seriously. 

 The Riksbank had been concerned that because of its strong impact on import prices, the weakening crown would boost inflation above its goal of two percent over a 12-24 month rolling horizon. 

 The underlying inflation index, which the central bank closely monitors in its interest rate decisions jumped to a seven-year high of 3.1 percent in May. 

 The bank said it sold 300 million euros and $190 million on June 15, a further 170 million euros and $240 million on June 18 and another 100 million euros and $200 million on June 25. 

 "Following the interventions there were no clear signs of rising inflation, higher inflation expectations or increased long-term interest rate differentials in relation to other countries," the Riksbank said in the minutes. 

 "Nor has the depreciation of the crown accelerated, rather the reverse. This indicates that the credibility of the inflation target has certainly not been affected negatively." 

 To reinforce the effects of the interventions, the central bank raised the key repo rate by 25 basis points to 4.25 percent in July at a time when many other central banks were cutting theirs to help slowing economies. 

 "The dramatic depreciation of the crown ceased after the interventions in June and the repo rate hike in July. The crown appreciated slightly until mid-August, when new data and developments on the financial markets indicated that the economic slowdown in Sweden and abroad would be more pronounced," the Riksbank said. 

 "Inflation expectations, when measured according to Statistics Sweden's survey of household purchasing plans, also fell slightly. The indications of weaker economic activity probably contributed to the latter." 

 Since June 2000 the crown has weakened by 24 percent against the dollar and 15 percent against the euro as foreign investors pulled out of the technology-laden Stockholm bourse and Swedish pension funds invested more abroad, taking advantage of new regulations.

title: Sweden  Riksbank Minutes: Future  Interventions  Possible
text:
STOCKHOLM -(Dow Jones)- Lars Heikensten, first deputy governor of Sweden's Riksbank, concluded at the central bank's Nov. 8 executive board meeting that it is possible  the Riksbank may intervene on the foreign exchange market again. 

 The minutes of that meeting, published Friday, revealed that all board members supported his conclusions, of which future possible intervention was one feature. 

 Heikensten said that, normally, interventions are made as a part of monetary policy and are aimed at safeguarding the inflation target. However, one can't rule out the possibility that other situations could arise where interventions may be motivated. It should always be possible to provide clear motives for such decisions, he added. 

 "Interventions are an instrument that will be used with great caution, as long as the floating exchange rate regime prevails," Heikensten said. 

 Normally, monetary policy is implemented through adjustments to the steering interest rates. 

 Situations where interventions are necessary are rarely obvious from a decision-making perspective, he said. It is therefore possible to have differing opinions within the executive board when making decisions on interventions. 

 Heikensten said the process for drafting and making decisions on interventions should be as open and clear as possible. 

 "This should be the starting point for proposals put to the executive board on procedures and communication, etc. regarding interventions," he said. 

 The discussion followed the Riksbank's series of interventions in the foreign exchange market in July, when it sold euros to the value of SEK12 billion. 

 Although the Riksbank carried out the interventions as part of its monetary policy, aimed at safeguarding price stability in line with the inflation target one to two years ahead, some uncertainty arose on the financial markets, as well as criticism among economists and other market participants. 

 The minutes of the Nov. 8 meeting stated that the Riksbank's credibility wasn't negatively affected by the interventions, when one considers the concept of credibility to refer to the inflation target and whether the measures taken contributed to achieving this or not. 

 "Following the interventions there were no clear signs of rising inflation, higher inflation expectations or increased long-term interest rate differentials in relation to other countries. Nor has the depreciation of the krona accelerated, rather the reverse. This indicates that the credibility of the inflation target has certainly not been affected negatively," the minutes said. 

 The Riksbank minutes noted also that many analysts, both market participants and academic research economists, have been critical of the measures taken and that this criticism has remained for longer than it did, for instance, after the Riksbank's last foreign exchangeinterventions in 1998.

title: Swedish c.banker casts doubts over crown defence.
text:
STOCKHOLM, Sept 4 (Reuters) - Monetary policy alone is not enough to quench big financial market swings, a board member of Sweden's central bank, which has recently intervened and raised key interest rates to prop up the ailing crown, said on Tuesday. 

 Eva Srejber, second deputy governor of the Riksbank and a member of its monetary-policy-setting executive board, said she did not believe "that monetary policy alone can counteract exaggerated movements in the financial markets". 

 Citing budding inflationary pressures from what it described at the time as an excessively weak crown exchange rate, the Riksbank intervened in the currency markets in June buying crowns against the euro and the dollar . 

 In July Sweden's central bank, which targets inflation of on average two percent over a business cycle, tightened monetary policy and justified the move by saying the persistently weak crown could pose a threat to the inflation target. 

 Measured by a trade-weighted currency basket index , the crown stood at 139.70 at 0745 GMT, just off all-time lows of 139.99 set on Monday but around one percent softer than in early July when the Riksbank raised its repo rate and in mid-June when the bank intervened to prop up the crown. 

 "A clear monetary policy aimed at price stability is necessary in the work on maintaining financial stability," Srejber said in the text of a prepared speech, which did not mention the Riksbank's actions regarding the crown.

title: Swedish PM sees fundamentals underpinning crown.
text:
NORRKOPING, Sweden, Aug 23 (Reuters) - Prime Minister Goran Persson said on Thursday his Social Democratic government's firm fiscal policy and Sweden's healthy economic fundamentals should positively underpin the recently ailing crown currency. 

 "We are conducting a firm fiscal policy, our inflation is low and we are competitive. That ought to give those who are watching the crown a positive picture of the Swedish currency," Persson told a news conference. 

 The Swedish unit hit all-time lows close to 9.50 crowns per euro earlier this week, marking a slide of six percent in the past three months, eight percent year-to-date and 18 percent from its record highs set in May last year. 

 At 1630 GMT on Thursday, it was trading around 9.44 per euro. 

 "It is politically opportunistic to believe, as the right-wing (opposition) parties do, that you can launch some kind of programme to shore up the crown exchange rate," Persson said, underlining that the crown was floating freely and that it was up to market forces to determine its external value. 

Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, intervened repeatedly in the foreign exchange market in June, justifying its support purchases of crowns for euros and dollars by saying the domestic unit's depreciation could threaten its two-percent inflation target. 

 Persson reiterated that he could not exclude Swedish membership of the euro by 2005 and said the entry requirement of two years of exchange rate stability would not be a problem. 

 "It is a factor that must be assessed. But it is a long time until then, we will make it," he said. 

 Persson said it was premature to begin discussing at what exchange rate the Swedish crown should be pegged to the euro although he noted that the issue would be important for the Swedish export industry. 

 The Social Democrats have promised to let the people decide the issue of euro membership in a referendum on an unspecified date.

title: UPDATE 1-Swedish June trade surplus hits all-time highs.
text:
STOCKHOLM, July 27 (Reuters) - Sweden's trade surplus rose to 15.4 billion crowns ($1.45 billion) in June - the largest surplus on record for any month since the launch in 1975 of the current method of collecting the data. 

 "It's the biggest figure ever," an official at Statistics Sweden (SCB), the national statistics office, told Reuters on Friday. 

 Exports rose to 66.0 billion crowns from 65.8 billion a year earlier, but were below May's 67.2 billion. Imports fell to 50.6 billion crowns, the lowest monthly figure since July 2000, from 53.3 billion and 54.8 billion respectively. 

 Swedish trade with fellow European Union countries generated a surplus of 1.9 billion crowns in June while trade with the rest of the world contributed 13.5 billion crowns. 

 The 0.3 percent year-on-year rise in exports defied analyst's expectations that they are set on a downward trend because of the slowdown in the world economy. 

 In June 2000, Sweden's economy was expanding at 4.6 percent, or double the pace in Q1 this year. 

 "We had expected a fall in exports...The weak crown can be an explanation why exports are going strong although demand is falling globally," said Johan Javeus, an analyst at Handelsbanken. 

 CROWN DOWN SIX PCT THIS YEAR 

 Measured by a trade-weighted currency basket index , the Swedish crown has fallen six percent this year and 15 percent in the past 12 months. The crown has dropped almost 25 percent against the globally firmer U.S. dollar . 

 The crown's slide prompted Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, to intervene last month in the currency markets by purchasing crowns in an effort to turn the weakening trend, which it said threatened its two-percent inflation target. 

 On July 5, the Riksbank raised key interest rates by a quarter point to 4.25 percent in a move it said was aimed at curbing inflationary pressures caused by the weaker crown. 

 A depreciating crown makes Swedish goods relatively cheaper to buy on international markets while importers in Sweden must spend more crowns on their purchases of goods from abroad. 

 In the first half of 2001 Swedish exports rose one percent year-on-year while imports grew three percent. The trade surplus dipped to 64.0 billion crowns from 69.6 billion in January-June 2000, the SCB said. 

 The National Institute of Economic Research (KI), an influential Swedish think-tank, said on Thursday industrial activity had weakened further in April-June with firms reporting a decline in order inflow from domestic and export markets. 

 "Export prices are estimated to drop slightly," the KI said, citing expectations among the companies it had surveyed. 

 Also on Thursday, the SCB said Swedish export prices had risen 2.2 percent year-on-year in June compared with a 6.9 percent advance in import prices. (Additional reporting by Anders Hultman in Stockholm).

title: Goldman Sachs sees Swedish crown strengthening.
text:
STOCKHOLM, July 19 (Reuters) - Investment bank Goldman Sachs said on Thursday the Swedish crown seemed to have broken out of its recent weakening spiral and was going to strengthen. 

 "Despite the weakness in the Swedish economy it looks as though the fundamental capital flows have turned in the crown's favour," Goldman Sachs said in a weekly foreign exchange analysis. 

 Goldman Sachs sees the Swedish currency firming to 8.80 against the euro on a 12-month horizon compared with 9.2450 at 1250 GMT. 

 "We would expect the crown to appreciate on a trade-weighted basis in coming months," it said. "Overall, crown weakness seems to have passed. 

 At 1250 GMT, Sweden's inverted trade-weighted currency basket index was 0.2 percent up on the day near three-week highs. 

 It was 1.6 percent up on all-time lows set in mid-June but 5.9 percent down so far in 2001 and 15 percent off year-on-year. 

 Repeated support interventions by Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, in the currency markets last month and its 25 basis point key rate rise to 4.25 percent early in July did not turn the crown onto a stronger path, but Goldman Sachs said the measures had not been in vain. 

 "In recent weeks the tightening of monetary policy combined with intervention by the Riksbank and a much healthier broad balance of payments position have helped to slow the crown's depreciating trend," it said. 

 Reflecting pension reform, which allowed pension funds to allocate more to foreign equities, Swedes have bought 96.5 billion crowns worth of foreign stocks in first five months of 2001, up from 4.9 billion crowns over the same period a year. 

 "Back in November we estimated that total pension reform outflow could be 84 billion crowns and if this is accurate it looks like most of the reform has already been done," Goldman Sachs said.

title: No respite seen for Swedish crown despite rate hike.
text:
LONDON, July 6 (Reuters) - The crown fell to record lows against the dollar after Sweden's central bank hiked interest rates on Friday and was expected to remain in the dog house with the Riksbank fighting a losing battle to prop up its currency. 

 Several bouts of crown-buying intervention by the Riksbank, Sweden's central bank, have failed to give the Swedish crown any lasting support, prompting the bank to raise its key rate a quarter point to 4.25 percent earlier in the day. 

 The central bank has expressed its concern that the crown's weakness is fuelling inflation, which is already at a seven-year high and well above the central bank's two percent one-two year target range. 

 But analysts said the Riksbank was fighting a losing battle. They added that the quarter-point rate hike was not enough to reverse capital outflows that have hurt the Swedish crown and the Riksbank was unable to tighten monetary policy further when growth was slowing. 

 "The Riksbank is in a no-win situation where it would have been damned if it hiked rates and damned if it didn't," said David Brown, chief economist at Bear Stearns International in London. 

 "The fact that intervention hasn't worked means the Riksbank has resorted to monetary tightening to control inflation but it is fighting a losing battle." 

 The Riksbank said last month that it would hike rates if intervention on the foreign exchanges did not succeed in halting crown weakness. 

 Brown said the Swedish crown was set for further weakness and expected the currency to test 9.40 against the euro over the next three months. The crown hit 2-1/2 year lows against the euro around 9.34 last month, before the first of the Riksbank's three bouts of intervention in its support. 

 Brown's forecast compares with three-day lows set around 9.27 per euro set earlier and came on a day when the euro had itself set eight-month troughs against the dollar. 

 RIKSBANK IN A CORNER 

 Sweden's currency has taken a hit from heavy capital outflows in recent months, following changes allowing Swedish pension funds to invest more overseas and recent weakness in Sweden's tech-laden stock market. 

 Against this backdrop, it was difficult for the Riksbank to take action to support the Swedish crown, analysts said. 

 Sweden's OMX stock index fell to its lowest in more than a week on Friday, hurt by recent profit warnings from European technology firms. 

 In Sweden, technology-related stocks account for just under half of the main stock market index, one of the highest concentrations in the world. 

 "There is a strong correlation between Sweden's stock exchange and the currency. Inward investment into Sweden has deteriorated sharply," said Hans Redeker, chief foreign exchange strategist at BNP Paribas in London. 

 Redeker said the crown was likely to weaken towards 9.45 against the euro in the next couple of months. 

 GROWTH WORRIES 

 Analysts said the Riksbank's rate increase could also weigh on the Swedish crown by exacerbating concerns about growth. 

 The Riksbank is one of the only central banks that has not cut rates this year in the face of a global slowdown. The Federal Reserve has cut rates six times and the European Central Bank, which like the Riksbank faces high inflation, has trimmed rates once. 

 "It is clear that intervention hasn't worked and that the Riksbank needed to hike rates to keep its credibility with markets," said Ryan Shea, international economist at Bank One in London. 

 "But Sweden's economy is slowing and a rate rise is perceived as a bad thing by investors." 

 The Riksbank expects the Swedish economy to grow 2.2 percent in 2001 and 2.5 percent in 2002. 

 Traders added that further rate increases, by raising costs for firms, would put more pressure on Swedish stocks and thereby the crown. 

 "Markets think 25 basis points is not enough to stabilise the crown so will price in higher rates, which is bad for equity markets," said Redeker from BNP Paribas. 

 Analysts said that further intervention from the Riksbank might provide some brief support for the crown, while any signs that the Riksbank was unlikely to intervene again could weigh heavily on the currency. 

 "If the Riksbank doesn't come in again, the market could see the Swedish crown as a one-way bet," said Bank One's Shea. 

 The crown has been in a downtrend against the euro since May 2000, when it hit highs around 8.0430 - over 10 percent stronger than current levels. It has also been on a downtrend against the dollar since 1996 when it hit highs around 6.4250 crown per dollar - more than 40 percent stronger than current levels.

title: Swedish crown woes may worsen if Riksbank hikes.
text:
LONDON, July 3 (Reuters) - The Swedish crown could suffer if the country's central bank, the Riksbank, raises interest rates this week in a bid to rescue a currency which has failed to draw much lasting benefit from repeated rounds of intervention. 

 While the Riksbank is expected to leave rates unchanged at Thursday's policy meeting, with an announcement due on Friday, it said last month that it would hike rates if intervention in the currency markets did not suceed in halting crown weakness. 

 Its intervention to buy crowns for dollars and euros on June 15, 18 and 25 has not been able to break an entrenched downtrend in the crown which has headed back toward record lows against the dollar and 2-1/2 year lows against the euro. 

 While some wonder whether the central bank could tighten policy as soon as this week, currency analysts said the move would only undermine the crown by exacerbating an economic slowdown already underway in Sweden. 

 "Option one of currency intervention failed and option two of raising rates could prove to be negative for the crown, especially in the current global environment where economic activity is slowing," said Neil MacKinnon, senior currency strategist at Merrill Lynch. "We'll see a negative impact on the economy from any rate hike and that is hardly a recipe to attract portfolio flows into the crown." 

 MacKinnon forecast the crown at 9.35 on a one-month horizon against the euro, just beyond a 2-1/2 year trough set on June 7. He saw the crown weakening beyond 11.00 against the dollar. This would take it close to record low of 11.0440 set on June 11. 

 The crown has been in a downtrend against the euro since May 2000, when it hit highs around 8.0430 - over 10 percent stronger than current levels. It has been on a downtrend against the dollar since 1996 when it hit highs around 6.4250 crown per dollar - more than 40 percent stronger than current levels. 

 Seven of 10 analysts surveyed by Reuters last week expected the Riksbank to leave rates steady on Friday, while three forecast a 25 basis point rate rise. 

 CHANGING TRENDS DIFFICULT 

 Traders said it would be difficult to change the trend in a currency that had been hit by real outflows of funds from the country rather than just poor sentiment. 

 Change in Sweden's pension funds industry this year has been a key factor in the crown's weakness as funds are now allowed to invest in foreign assets. 

 Also, weakness in technolgy stocks this year has hurt the crown which tends to track Sweden's tech-laden stock market. 

 With Swedish economic data beginning to deteriorate in the current economic climate, a rate rise would only serve to harm the economy and hence the currency, analysts said. 

 But with underlying inflation, the gauge upon which the Swedish central bank bases its monetary policy, hitting a seven-year high of 3.1 percent year on year in May, the Riksbank's options are looking limited and tough. 

 "The downward pressure on the Swedish crown is coming from portflio flows and not speculators," said Jesper Dannesboe, chief currency strategist at Dresdner Kleinwort Wasserstein. 

 "The best the Riksbank could hope for is for the crown to consolidate in a range. To hike rates in a context of domestic economy weakening will not be welcomed so maybe it would be better not to move rates and just intervene." 

 Riksbank is one of the only central banks that has not cut interest rates this year in the face of a global slowdown. It's key repo rate was last changed in December when it was raised by a quarter percentage point to 4.00 percent. 

 In contrast, the U.S. Federal Reserve has slashed 2.75 percentage points off the fed funds target rate so far this year. Even the European Central Bank, which is faced with rising inflation, has cut euro zone interest rates by 25 basis points. 

 Chartists said the crown would need to strengthen almost four percent against the euro before the technical outlook turned brighter. 

 "The euro/crown's trend is up, up and up," said Steve Wesiak, technical strategist at ABN AMRO in Amsterdam. "The major part of the uptrend started in May 2000 and to break that you would need to take out 8.90."

title: UPDATE 2-Swedish finmin says crown  intervention  will work.
text:
STOCKHOLM, June 27 (Reuters) - Swedish Finance Minister Bosse Ringholm said on Wednesday he believed recent foreign exchange interventions by the Riksbank central bank would succeed in supporting the Swedish crown. 

 "Absolutely," he told Reuters on the sidelines of a conference. "We have a quite independent central bank in Sweden. It's up to the Riksbank to decide, but of course I hope the intervention will be successful in strengthening the Swedish crown." 

 The crown reversed early weakness against the euro and the dollar in the wake of his remarks, but remained weaker than when the Riksbank started buying earlier in the month. 

Foreign exchange markets have continued to test the Riksbank's resolve, driving Sweden's currency further into territory last seen before the Riksbank started buying. 

 CROWN AND EURO "UNDERVALUED" 

 Asked if the euro was undervalued, Ringholm, who is also the current head of the European Union's Ecofin group of finance ministers, said: "Yes, I suppose both the euro and the Swedish crown will be stronger in the future because the economic situation in Europe and Sweden is strong just now." 

 The Riksbank has repeatedly intervened to support the Swedish crown against the dollar and the euro in recent sessions in a bid to repel inflationary pressures. 

 Its purchases temporarily stemmed a weakening trend in the currency but have failed to provide substantial support. 

 The crown pared early losses to last trade at 10.672 to the dollar against 10.685 late on Tuesday and 9.225 to the euro from around 9.238. 

 The Riksbank has said the falling crown threatens its two percent inflation target, with Swedish headline inflation hitting a six-year high of 3.0 percent year-on-year in May. Underlying inflation, which is the main gauge monitored by the Riksbank, hit a seven-year high of 3.1 percent. 

 But Ringholm said he was not overly concerned by the latest data. 

 "In the last few months we have seen higher inflation in Sweden and Europe but at the same time there are special reasons for that so I don't think it is necessary to make final conclusions," he said. 

 "We will have to see in four, five or six months if it is more permanent inflation," he said. "In Sweden we have had very successful wage negotiations... so it is a good situation for calm inflation developments in the future."

title: Swedish crown jumps, no c.bank activity seen.
text:
LONDON, June 21 (Reuters) - The Swedish crown jumped against the euro and the dollar on Thursday, but traders said they had not seen the Swedish central bank buying crowns. 

 The Riksbank, Sweden's central bank, subsequently said it had not been intervening following forays to buy Swedish crowns last Friday and again on Monday. 

 Traders blamed illiquid and nervous markets for the sudden crown move, following the European Central Bank's decision to leave interest rates unchanged. 

 "The move has been exaggerated as markets are extremely thin," said Mark Henry, currency strategist at GNI. 

 The Swedish crown rose by a third of a percent to 9.13 against the euro from levels around 9.16 in the space of a few minutes, and also rallied to 10.66 against the dollar from around 10.69.

title: Swedish c.bank says has not  intervened  in  forex .
text:
STOCKHOLM, June 21 (Reuters) - Sweden's Riksbank central bank said it had not intervened in the forex market on Thursday after the crown spiked sharply against the euro and the dollar. 

 "We have not been into the market today," Riksbank spokesman Thomas Thyblad said. 

 The Riksbank had previously intervened on Friday and Monday to support the domestic currency, which it regards as distinctly undervalued. 

 On Friday it said the strategy was a monetary policy action to combat the inflationary impact of an excessively weak currency. 

 Riksbank Governor Urban Backstrom said on Saturday he believed the crown's weakening by double-digit percentage figures against the euro and the dollar in the past year, a trend which has recently accelerated, was due largely to a market psychology, which he likened to the boom and bust in information technology shares in 1999-2000. 

 "This can feed on itself and that's why we wanted to enter the market with full strength and send a signal that this is wrong," he said in an interview on Swedish radio news.

title: Swedish c.bank says buys crowns in  FX intervention .
text:
STOCKHOLM, June 18 (Reuters) - Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, said on Monday it intervened in the foreign exchange market buying Swedish crowns. 

 "We have intervened and bought crowns," a Riksbank spokesman said. 

 The crown spiked sharply against the euro and firmed slightly against the dollar . 

 The Riksbank had intervened on behalf of the domestic currency, which it regards as distinctly undervalued, already on Friday in what it said was a monetary policy action to combat the inflationary impact of an excessively weak currency. 

 The Riksbank stressed last week that it did not have any exchange rate target for the crown but was only intent on preventing currency weakness from hindering its efforts to steer inflation back towards its two percent target.

title: UPDATE 2-Swedish c.bank  intervenes , crown climbs.
text:
STOCKHOLM, June 18 (Reuters) - Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, intervened in the foreign exchange market on Monday for the second trading day in a row by buying Swedish crowns, pushing the Swedish currency up against the dollar and the euro. 

 "We have intervened and bought crowns," a Riksbank spokesman said. He declined to comment on volumes, against which currency and at what level the bank had intervened. 

Currency dealers and analysts said the Riksbank had been in the market buying crowns against both the euro and the dollar. 

 The Riksbank had already intervened on behalf of the domestic currency - which it regards as distinctly undervalued - on Friday in what it said was a monetary policy action to combat the inflationary impact of an excessively weak currency. 

 The crown jumped by 0.8 percent against the euro and by 1.1 percent, against the dollar in the wake of Monday afternoon's central bank action, but later eased somewhat. 

 The crown, which hit on Monday its firmest levels against both the euro and the dollar since May 25, has now strengthened by 3.8 percent against the dollar and by 2.3 percent versus the euro compared with levels last Thursday afternoon before Governor Urban Backstrom warned in a speech that intervention could not be ruled out. 

 Dealers said the Riksbank had been buying crowns on Monday against the euro at around 9.07-9.10 crowns per euro and later at 10.60 and firmer levels against the U.S. currency. 

 FOUR PERCENT OF RESERVES 

 Dealers estimated that Monday's interventions totalled around 300 million euros, or roughly the same amount as on Friday. 

 Guillaume Salomon, an analyst at UBS Warburg, told Reuters it seemed that the Riksbank had spent around four percent of its foreign exchange reserves in its repeated interventions on Friday and Monday. 

 "Initially, what they want to do is to break the trend," Salomon said, referring to the Riksbank's stated purpose for the interventions. 

 The Swedish central bank does not have an exchange rate target for the freely floating crown. But it has said that the steady weakening until Friday of the exchange rate is posing a threat to its two percent inflation target. 

 Riksbank Governor Urban Backstrom said on Saturday he believed the crown's weakening by double-digit percentage figures against the euro and the dollar in the past year, a trend which has recently accelerated, was due largely to a market psychology, which he likened to the boom and bust in information technology shares in 1999-2000. 

 "This can feed on itself and that's why we wanted to enter the market with full strength and send a signal that this is wrong," he said in an interview on Swedish radio news. 

 SHOWING THE FLAG 

 "We wanted to show the currency market, hoist the flag, that something is odd with the Swedish crown." 

 Mans Grunberger, a currency analyst at SEB Merchant Banking, told Reuters it was difficult to say whether the Riksbank would be back in the market again later this week. 

 "The Riksbank has shown that it is very determined to strengthen the crown so it (more intervention) cannot be excluded," he said. 

 "It is hard to say if there will be more support purchases because they are now back at the crown levels that prevailed at the time of the latest inflation report when the bank did not express any worries about the crown," said John Kyriakopoulus, a currency strategist at JP Morgan. 

 At 1455 GMT the crown was quoted at 9.0525 against the euro and at 10.5085 per dollar compared with 9.1209 and 10.5951 respectively at midsession. 

 The Riksbank stressed last week it did not have any exchange rate target for the crown but was intent on preventing currency weakness from hindering its efforts to steer inflation back towards its two percent target. 

 Swedish headline inflation hit a six-year high of 3.0 percent year-on-year in May with underlying inflation, which is the main gauge monitored by the Riksbank, at a seven-year high of 3.1 percent. 

 "It is the crown's development which has caused the inflation risks to look somewhat different now," Backstrom said in the radio interview. (Additional reporting by Johan Sennero and Jenny Andersson in Stockholm).

title: Nordic stocks trade sideways, Statoil debut flat.
text:
STOCKHOLM, June 18 (Reuters) - Norway's Statoil dribbled back to its IPO at the end of its first day of trade on Monday, setting the tone for flat Nordic markets, while Finland's Elcoteq dropped 14 percent on a profit warning. 

 Renewed profit worries, looming regional holidays and wariness ahead of results from U.S. software maker Oracle reduced trading in Nordic stocks to a near-torpor. 

 "The trade is pathetic because buyers are starting their summer holidays," one Helsinki broker said. 

 "There is a lot of nervousness around technology earnings and that will continue to weigh on the sector," a Copenhagen dealer said. 

 The region's benchmark Stoxx Nordic index was down 0.03 percent as two off the region's four bourses closed, outperforming the FTSE Eurotop 300 index by half a percent. 

 Finnish telecoms equipment heavyweight Nokia - which last week was rocked by major selloffs after a profit warning - was down half a percent, with investors weighing the implications of after a warning from Canadian rival Nortel Networks on Friday.. 

 "Nortel's profit-warning was bad news for Nokia, but not as bad as some first thought," a broker said. 

 "The mentality in general is that no positive news is anticipated, instead the market hopes for as few profit warnings this week as possible," another said. 

 Swedish competitor Ericsson shed 2.7 percent. 

 STATOIL SHEDS EARLY GAINS 

 Norwegian oil company Statoil opened at 72 crowns, above its IPO level, as the Nordic region's biggest listing since that of Swedish telecom operator Telia got under way. But profit takers pushed the stock back to its listing price. 

 Analysts said the share issue - which had been four times oversubscribed - supported the view that a tentative recovery in the IPO market was gathering momentum. 

 "It's a huge amount of money and it's healthy that most of the issue, about 78 percent, was bought by investors outside Norway," said Danske Securities oil analyst Bjorn Jacobsen. 

 Nokia and Ericsson supplier Elcoteq dived into the red as much as 19 percent at its intraday low after the company warned weaker market conditions would force it to post a "clear loss" in the second quarter. 

 Forestry stocks were mixed. Investors continued to weigh the impact of a profit warning by Finnish papermaker M-Real last week and the effect on dollar-earning companies of forex market intervention by Sweden's central bank on Friday and Monday, which pushed up the value of the crown. 

 Brokers said the market had priced in 1 weak crown and the impact of a Riksbank intervention on Swedish paper stocks - many of whom have big operations in the U.S. and products priced in dollars - saw some investors offload positions. 

 Swedish groups Holmen and Assi Doman , which were off Friday, fell again by 0.7 percent and half a percent respectively. 

 "The intervention, in combination with the profit warning (by M-Real), had some kind of trigger effect and there was some profit taking in those shares," said a Swedish head trader. 

 But fund managers said share prices in the sector had come off recently. "Valuations are reasonably cheap at the moment and buying on weakness is probably a good idea," said Gregor Smith at Aberdeen Asset Management. 

 (Additional reporting by Helsinki newsroom, Copenhagen newsroom, Oslo newsroom).

title: Riksbank unsure of  intervention  success - governor.
text:
STOCKHOLM, June 16 (Reuters) - The governor of Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, said on Saturday it was premature to say whether Friday's currency market interventions, which saw the crown currency reverse a recent weakening trend, would achieve its purpose of staving off a growing inflation threat. 

 "As a central bank you can never know if interventions succeed or not but we have a quite considerable currency reserve and we are acting with full strength," Urban Backstrom said in a radio interview. 

 "It was good that it happened," he said, referring to the Swedish currency's advance to two-week highs against both the dollar and the euro on Friday. 

 "It is difficult to draw conclusions after the development over only one or two days, this is a longer perspective and we will have to see how it develops going forward." 

 Backstrom also told Swedish public radio the intervention had been aimed at containing inflation and did not rule out raising key interest rates. 

 "I don't want to say anything concrete...we'll have to see when the time comes for us to do that. But we are below many other central banks which have cut rates and we are below the European Central Bank's (ECB) rate," he said. 

 "I don't want to bind myself on exactly how much it would be, in such a case (that the Riksbank were to raise rates)," he added. 

 He said the Riksbank's foreign exchange reserves - approximately 160 billion crowns ($15 billion) - were substantial. 

 According to dealer estimates, Friday's interventions were in the region of three billion crowns. Dealers told Reuters on Friday the Riksbank had bought crowns for around 9.19-9.21 and later 9.1250-9.1450 per euro and also for about 10.58 per dollar . 

 The Riksbank confirmed on Friday it had intervened but declined to say by how much or at what levels which currencies had been sold. 

 Sweden's key repo rate has been on hold at 4.00 percent since early December when it was raised by 25 basis points. The ECB's main refi rate was cut to 4.50 percent from 4.75 percent this spring. 

 The Riksbank's executive board will hold its next monetary policy board meeting on July 5. 

 BOOM AND BUST 

 Backstrom said he believed that the crown's weakening by double-digit percentage figures against the euro and the dollar in the past year, a trend which has recently accelerated, was due largely to a market psychology, which he likened to the boom and bust in information technology shares in 1999-2000. 

 "It's a 'follow-the-leader' behaviour in the currency market where operators are acting not on the basis of the outlook for the Swedish economy but according to what they think others are doing," he said. 

 "This can feed on itself and that's why we wanted to enter the market with full strength and send a signal that this is wrong," he said. 

 "We wanted to show the currency market, hoist the flag, that something is odd with the Swedish crown." 

 Backstrom reiterated that the Riksbank, although convinced the crown is undervalued, did not target any particular exchange rate for the currency and that the purpose of the intervention had been to combat the inflationary pressure caused by the crown's depreciating external value. 

 "It is the crown's development which has caused the inflation risks to look somewhat different now," he said. 

 A soft currency leads to higher prices of imported goods, in the current environment especially meat and petroleum products, the governor said. 

 WEAK CROWN HITS CONSUMERS 

 "It is completely clear that a falling crown exchange rate affects people's wallets," he said. "If the crown remains at a low level there is a risk of price effects elsewhere in our economy." 

 Unwavering action by the Riksbank was important from the point of view of maintaining the broad support and credibility enjoyed by the low-inflation policy. If the public's inflation expectations shifted upwards, "a price and wage spiral sets off again," he said. 

 "We will do our utmost to make sure that inflation remains at two percent," Backstrom said, stressing the longer-term nature of the Riksbank's monetary policy goal of on average two percent over a business cycle, which implies that monetary policy adjustments can be expected to take effect on a 12-24 month horizon. 

 Swedish headline inflation hit a six-year high of 3.0 percent year-on-year in May with underlying inflation, which is the main gauge monitored by the Riksbank, at a seven-year high of 3.1 percent. 

 "Now we have a situation where we lie above the inflation target. What is important is that we systematically aim at two percent when we conduct our policy," Backstrom said. 

 "Of course we could make sure that inflation would be next month exactly two percent by dramatically pulling the interest rate trigger. If we now quickly raise the rate to, say 15-20 percent, it could have rapid effects on inflation but this creates great instability for employment and production in the Swedish economy and people would soon lose confidence in the Riksbank's actions," he said.

title: UPDATE 3-Swedish c.bank  intervention  beefs up crown.
text:
STOCKHOLM, June 15 (Reuters) - Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, intervened repeatedly in foreign exchange markets on Friday to support the domestic crown currency and stave off a growing inflationary threat. 

 The crown jumped against both the dollar and the euro and was holding near two-week highs by 1600 GMT, though slightly off intra-day peaks corresponding to gains of 1.5 percent and 1.1 percent against the dollar and the euro respectively. 

 But despite the currency's advance analysts said the intervention, a rare move these days by central banks targeting inflation rather than exchange rates, may not achieve its purpose unless backed up by a rise in key interest rates. 

 "In this environment the probability of a hike in the near term increases very substantially," UBS Warburg analyst Guillaume Salomon said in a research note. 

 Swedish Finance Minister Bosse Ringholm said he hoped the interventions would be successful. 

 But Ringholm, current chairman of the European Union's Ecofin grouping of finance ministers, said he believed the Riksbank's move was not intended as a signal to the European Central Bank (ECB) to act in a similar way to support the weak euro. 

 "It is up to the Riksbank to decide about such things... but of course when the Riksbank makes these interventions the government is hoping that it will be successful," Ringholm told reporters after an Ecofin meeting during a summit of EU leaders in Gothenburg in south-western Sweden. 

 Sweden is not a member of the euro single currency. 

 POLICY REVIEW ON JULY 5 

 The Riksbank said in a statement it had intervened "with a view to strengthening the Swedish crown" but declined to comment on levels or currencies sold. 

 "The Riksbank will make a complete assessment of inflation and the consequences for monetary policy at the Executive Board meeting on 5 July,", the central bank said. 

 Swedish short-term market interest rates spiked up as investors began discounting a monetary tightening. The benchmark six-month maturity jumped 13 basis points to 4.30 percent. 

 "They (the Riksbank) could do without the interest rate gap against the ECB," Aisling Freiheit-Kinch, an analyst at Morgan Stanley in New York, told Reuters. 

 "The question is now are they willing to back it up with interest rate hikes?" 

 She said the 50 basis point differential between the Riksbank's repo rate at 4.00 percent and the European Central Bank's (ECB) main refi rate at 4.50 percent was one reason why funds had continued to flow out of Sweden, putting pressure on the crown. 

Foreign exchange dealers said the Riksbank had been buying crowns against the euro at 9.19-9.21 crowns and at 10.58 crowns against the dollar during the morning session and again against the euro at 9.1250-9.1450 in the afternoon. 

 The euro leapt a quarter cent to new three-week highs of $0.8673 according to Reuters data, its best showing since May 22, and up more than 1/2 a cent on the day, with traders attributing the move to the talk of sales of dollars for Swedish crowns by the Riksbank. 

 At 1605 GMT the euro was trading at $0.8620. 

 ADVANCE WARNING 

Sweden's intervention came one day after a warning by Urban Backstrom, the Riksbank governor, that this was a tool that could be used. 

 "The Riksbank warned of their intentions yesterday, so the market should not be surprised," said Steve Barrow, currency strategist at Bear Stearns in London. 

 "The crown's weakness is jeopardising price stability and the Riksbank is likely to keep intervening until the crown has stabilised," he added. 

 The Riksbank does not have an exchange rate target for the freely floating crown but has said currency market intervention is a tool at its disposal to combat inflation, which hit a six-year high of 3.0 percent in May with underlying inflation at a seven-year high of 3.1 percent, both well above the bank's two percent target. 

 The Riksbank said the continued depreciation of the crown was increasing the risk of inflation exceeding the target. 

 "The risk of inflation has grown in that the krona has continued to depreciate from levels that were already low," it said in a statement. 

 "At a time when the exchange rate is a serious upside risk in the inflation forecast and deviates markedly from a reasonable value, a situation may arise where currency market interventions are motivated," Backstrom said on Thursday. 

 The crown climbed to 10.55, its highest in two weeks against the dollar, and stood at 10.5760 at 1605 GMT. 

 It also firmed to 9.1250 per euro before settling back at 9.1330 at 1605 GMT.

 Heikensten said the Riksbank had presented an inflation report on May 31 whose chief message was that in the period one to two years ahead - the main focus of monetary policy - inflation would be in line with the bank's two percent target. 

 "For a number of reasons, however, the picture was more uncertain than usual," Heikensten said. 

 Inflation figures presented on Thursday were in line with the Riksbank's assesment in May, Heikensten said. 

 "There is however one clear deviation from what we counted on. The Swedish crown has continued to weaken, which is the opposite of the assumptions on which the Inflation Report's main scenario is based." 

 Heikensten said that amounted to a shift in the spectrum of inflation risks. 

 If the exchange rate were to remain weak it could have consequences for monetary policy. 

 "... in a situtation where the exchange rate deviates from a reasonable value and simultaneously constitutes a risk for inflation, currency market interventions may be motivated," Heikensten added.

title: TEXT- Sweden 's Riksbank's statement on its  intervention .
text:
STOCKHOLM, June 15 (Reuters) - The Swedish Central Bank, the Riksbank, issued the following statement following its intervention in the foreign exchange market to support the crown. 

 "Today the Riksbank has intervened in the currency market with a view to strengthening the Swedish krona. The intervention is based on a decision taken by the Executive Board on 14 June. 

 It is judged that, since the publication of the latest Inflation Report the risk of inflation exceeding the Riksbank's 2 per cent target has increased. 

 In the Inflation Report, published on 31 May, it was considered that inflation one to two years ahead would be approximately in line with the target. The risk spectrum was balanced. At the same time, the uncertainty was unusually pronounced. 

 The new information about economic developments and inflation in Sweden and the rest of the world does not by itself motivate a change in the appraisal of inflation prospects one to two years ahead. Nevertheless, the risk of inflation has grown in that the krona has continued to depreciate from levels that were already low. 

 The Riksbank does not target the exchange rate. Monetary policy aims to maintain price stability. The target is two per cent inflation one to two years ahead. In the assessment of inflation, the exchange rate is an important factor. It directly affects import prices for intermediate and consumer goods and also has an indirect effect via inflation expectations and aggregate demand for Swedish goods. 

 The low exchange rate during a large part of the past decade has affected inflation but not as much as expected. A value of the krona that continues to be unduly low in the coming year will affect inflation prospects, particularly as resource utilisation is high. The krona's depreciation since the latest Inflation Report is the most important single factor that may lead to the inflation target being threatened 1-2 years from now. 

 One of the measures available to the Riksbank is currency-market intervention. This can be particularly motivated if pricing in the currency market deviates markedly from what can be considered fundamentally appropriate and if the price is moving away from what is fundamentally appropriate in a process that is liable to become self-generating. 

 The Riksbank will make a complete assessment of inflation and the consequences for monetary policy at the Executive Board meeting on 5 July."

title: EU SUMMIT:  Sweden  PM Backs Riksbank's Krona  Intervention
text:
GOTHENBURG, Sweden -(Dow Jones)- Swedish Prime Minister Goeran Persson said Friday that the country's central bank had his "full support" after it intervened to support the krona on foreign exchange markets. 

 "They (Swedish central bank officials) have my full support and I am confident about their ability," Persson told Dow Jones Newswires on the sidelines of a European Union summit meeting in Gothenburg. 

 Persson was responding to a question about his opinion of the intervention earlier Friday by the central bank, known as the Sveriges Riksbank. 

 As reported, Sveriges Riksbank confirmed it bought the local currency and sold U.S. dollars to prevent the krona's weakness from increasing inflationary pressures. 

 Persson went out of his way to praise the Riksbank even though he emphasized the bank is independent by law. 

 "I have no influence at all on the central bank," he said. "I think they are capable and they are professional. They know what they do and they are using the instruments they have." 

 Separately Friday, Swedish Finance Minister Bosse Ringholm said he hoped the Riksbank move would be "successful." 

 In remarks to reporters, Ringholm also said he didn't expect the Riksbank's intervention to affect the likelihood of intervention by the European Central Bank. 

 Analysts have seen ECB intervention as likely in recent weeks as the euro's foreign exchange rate fell to roughly six-month lows below $0.85. 

 "I think that it's an independent position by the Swedish Riksbank and the ECB will take its own position," Ringholm said. "I don't think it's necessary to have any form of coordination." 

 In any case, analysts expressed doubts that the Riksbank intervention would succeed.

text:
STOCKHOLM, June 14 (Reuters) - Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, said on Thursday it did not rule out intervention in the foreign exchange market if the crown remained weak and posed an upside inflation risk. 

 "The Riksbank considers that in a fundamental perspective, today's weak exchange rate is not reasonable," Riksbank Governor Urban Backstrom said in the extract of a speech. 

 "If the crown remains weak for a longer period, there may be risk of inflation being higher one to two years from now." 

 Earlier, Statistics Sweden (SCB) said consumer price inflation rose to a six-year high of 3.0 percent in May with underlying inflation, which forms the basis for the Riksbank's monetary policy, hitting a seven-year high of 3.1 percent. 

 The Riksbank's monetary policy target is two percent inflation on average over a business cycle. The target comes with a plus/minus one percentage point fluctuation band. 

 Backstrom said the interest rate was the primary instrument for a central bank with an inflation target. 

 "If there are grounds for believing that the crown will continue to be weak - and nothing else happens to alter inflation prospects - that will have consequences for monetary policy," he said. 

 But using the strongest and most direct language heard from the Riksbank since the crown began weakening against the euro a year ago and against the dollar in late 1999, Backstrom said currency intervention was another tool at a central bank's disposal. 

 "At a time when the exchange rate is a serious upside risk in the inflation forecast and deviates markedly from a reasonable value, a situation may arise where currency market interventions are motivated," Backstrom said. 

 The extract of his speech was titled "Currency interventions cannot be ruled out". 

 The crown has weakened by more than 17.5 percent against the dollar this year and by more than one-third since mid-October 1999. Against the euro, the Swedish currency has fallen by 16 percent in the past 12 months and by 6.5 percent so far this year. 

 At 1345 GMT the crown was trading at 9.2089 per euro compared with 9.2358 at midday after the May inflation report but before Backstrom's speech. The crown also advanced slightly versus the dollar, to 10.8276 from 10.8298.

title: Swedish c.bank has no plan to support crown - paper.
text:
STOCKHOLM, Feb 21 (Reuters) - Sweden's central bank, or Riksbank, has no plans to support the crown, which has weakened more than 10 percent in the past six months, Riksbank deputy governor Villy Bergstrom was quoted on Wednesday as saying. 

 "The issue is not even under discussion," Bergstrom told the financial daily Finanstidningen in an interview. 

 In autumn 1998, the Riksbank intervened in the foreign exchange market to support the crown. 

Sweden is a member of the European Union but has not joined the third phase of Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) and the euro single currency. The crown is a free-floating currency. 

 The Riksbank's trade-weighted currency basket TCW-index rose above 132 this month for the first time since July 1995. The higher the index, the weaker the crown. 

 At the time of the October 1998 intervention, the TCW-index hovered just above 130. 

 Bergstrom told Finanstidningen a continued softening of the currency entailed a certain inflation threat down the road. 

 "But on the other hand experience tells us that a weaker crown no longer has the same impact on inflation as earlier," he said. 

 The Riksbank's inflation target is two percent on average over a business cycle. In December, Swedish inflation fell to 1.4 percent year-on-year from 1.7 percent in November. 

 Bergstrom said the Riksbank's next key rate move could be up or down. The bank's next monetary policy board meeting is scheduled for March 26. 

 The Riksbank raised the repo rate to 4.00 percent from 3.75 percent in early December. 

 "At that time we believed in a series of rate increases this spring. But this sentiment has definitely turned," Bergstrom said. 

 "Now the March meeting will show where we are headed. If the supply side tightening continues an increase cannot be ruled out," he said. 

 "But it is clear that if there is a sharp (economic) downturn which hits our exports and if consumers begin to lose confidence, then it can be a (rate) cut," he added.

title: Market ructions seen limited as Danish vote nears.
text:
LONDON, Sept 27 (Reuters) - Financial markets will feel repurcussions from Thursday's closely-run Danish vote on euro membership, but the threat of coordinated intervention to support the euro is likely to limit any fallout. 

 With just one day left before Thursday's referendum, the race was still too close to call, though the majority of polls were predicting a "no" by the Danes. 

 A rejection risks being interpreted as a vote of no-confidence in the single currency project, making it a negative for the euro and euro zone assets, analysts said. 

 But any attempts to bid down the single currency would be made with great trepidation after last Friday's coordinated Group of Seven intervention to support the euro, the first such move since 1995. 

 "In the event of a "no" vote there will be some downside pressure on euro/dollar but the market will tread very, very carfully," said Claudio Piron, treasury economist at Standard Chartered Bank in London. 

 The euro was trading at around $0.8850 on Wednesday, near the top of its post-intervention trading range. 

 Traders have had a long time to get used to the idea of a rejection by the Danes, which in itself should limit their reaction, Piron said. 

 "I am looking for only a modest move, this has been talked to death by the markets." 

 The euro's performance, in turn, is the linchpin for any reaction on euro zone bond and stock markets, where a steep fall in the currency would prompt sympathetic downward moves. 

 Also hanging fire on the results are Denmark's own markets, which will be most directly affected, and bonds and currencies from euro candidates Britain and Sweden. 

INTERVENTION SAFETY NET FOR EURO 

 Traders and analysts have cited signs that Danish opposition to entry was hardening in recent weeks as one of the factors which assisted the euro's slide to record lows last week. 

 But all bets of how far the euro would fall if the Danes rejected euro entry are off after the Group of Seven industrial nations intervened in the single currency's support last week. 

 Concern the G7 will mount another joint euro-buying spree if the single currency comes under renewed pressure is expected to restrain euro bears' enthusiasm in the event of a rejection. 

 "If it is a no vote, would you sell euros if the ECB was going to be just around the corner?" said Steve Barrow, currency strategist at Bear Stearns International in London. 

 "Last week's intervention makes the vote more difficult to trade off." 

 Likewise, a "yes" vote is seen as having limited upside for the single currency and euro zone bonds. While Denmark is seen as generally fiscally solid, it represents only about two percent of the euro zone economic whole. In addition, Denmark is seen as likely foot-dragger on structural reform. 

 On bond markets, analysts held out the potential that a "no" vote would prompt flight to safety in core euro issuers such as Germany and France, with underperformance from Italy. But this will most likely be driven by euro falls, with a sharp independent move by the bond market seen as unlikely. 

 NO DRAMA FOR EURO OUTS 

 The outcome of the Danish referendum with the vote is seen swaying public opinion on euro entry in Britain and had, in recent months, been expected to influence the pound given any British euro entry is expected to occur at a weaker exchange rate than sterling is currently trading at. 

 But the pound has already become much less sensitive to the referendum as Britain's euro-friendly Labour government flagging political fortunes are seen making British entry into the single currency a more distant prospect. 

 The Swedish public is also expected to be influenced by the Danish vote but the Swedish crown is seen less liable to move violently in its wake. 

 DANISH ASSETS SEEN VULNERABLE BUT NO 1992 

 If "no" carries the day the sharpest moves may well be Danish markets. 

 Credit Lyonnais is expecting a no vote to drive Danish 10-year bond spreads over bunds to about 60 basis points from its current 41, as investors factor in currency risk and kiss convergence plays goodbye. 

 On the flip side, a "yes" will fuel a rally taking spreads eventually down to about 25 basis points, according to Credit Lyonnais. 

 The Danish crown will face selling pressure in the event of a rejection. 

 "In the case of a no the (Danish) central bank would have to prove once again that it means business," Unibank senior economist Anne Buchardt told Reuters Television. 

 "They will probably have to intervene and I guess they will have to raise rates as well." 

 Danish authorities have pledged to maintain the crown's fixed exchange rate link with the euro even if Danes reject the common currency. And the European Central Bank has vowed to "do everything in its power" to keep Denmark in Exchange Rate Mechanism-2. 

 Denmark's shock rejection of the Maastrict treaty in June 1992 cast a pall of uncertainty over Europe's push towards a single currency and undermined the European exchange rate mechanism (ERM). 

 This culminated in sterling and the Italian lira's ejection from the ERM in September, forcing the French to call a similar referendum. 

 But with the euro now a reality the project is far more resilient, analysts said. 

 (Additional reporting by Swaha Pattanaik in London).

title: FOCUS - Swedish Riksbank  intervenes , rescues crown.
text:
STOCKHOLM, Oct 7 (Reuters) - Sweden's Riksbank intervened in the foreign exchange market for the first time in at least a year on Wednesday, buying crowns for marks in a successful bid to stop the beleaguered currency from tracking the dollar's sharp decline. 

 Riksbank governor Urban Backstrom told a seminar in New York the central bank had intervened because the crown's recent sharp decline was unjustified by the economy's fundamentals. 

 "Under these circumstances the Riksbank has chosen to use currency interventions to underscore that the movements in the crown's exchange rate have been unduly abrupt and exaggerated," he said. It was the first confirmation the central bank had intervened. 

 Earlier, dealers said the Riksbank had bought crowns for marks several times, first at around 4.83 to the mark and later at 4.80. This halted an initial slide which took the Swedish currency to 4.9135 marks in the morning, approaching a three-year trough of 4.9420 to the mark hit on Monday. 

 The Riksbank has repeatedly said that the crown - which has lost more than 13 percent of its value against the mark so far this year - was undervalued. At 1640 GMT, it had weakened slightly to 4.8115 to the mark, compared with a day's trough of 4.7950 just after the latest intervention. 

 Analysts said the intervention made sense because the dollar hit 12-month lows against Germany's mark on Wednesday, a dive which some said could have taken the crown through the key 5.0 to the mark level. 

 "If there should ever be any reason for the Swedish central bank to intervene then today was the day," SE Banken strategist Georg Anderson told Reuters. 

 "It makes sense to break the relationship between the crown and dollar/mark because of the dollar's massive fall today - they have succeeded this time but whether they can do it again is another story," he said. 

 Analysts say that Sweden's economic fundamentals - which include low inflation, steady growth and gradual reduction of public debt - are solid, but the crown has been on the wrong side of recent global financial turbulence. 

 As long as investors remain frightened, they would sell against core European assets, which are protected by the onset of European economic and monetary union, economists say. 

 "The central bank needs to be more vigilant now and this is probably an early example - the only thing that worries me is that unless one thinks that global delirium has come to an end - this is just one round of intervention," Anderson said. 

 Economists say that that rate hikes in Denmark and Norway earlier this year were prompted by the failure of those countries' central banks to stem currency declines with intervention. 

 Backstrom noted that if the crown's exchange rate remained weak, inflation pressure could be generated which might affect the future path of monetary policy. 

 The Riksbank's inflation report published last week assumed that the repo rate, Sweden's main interest rate, would remain unchanged, he said. 

 "As the Swedish crown is judged to be undervalued at present, we also assume that the exchange rate follows a path that represents a gradual appreciation," he said. ((Stockholm newsroom, +46-8-700 1000, fax +46-8-211601, stockholm.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Sweden Riksbank Bought Kronor To Slow Softening - Traders
text:
OSLO (AP-Dow Jones)--According to Stockholm dealers the Riksbank, Sweden's central bank has intervened in the foreign exchange market Friday, buying kronor to damp volatility. 

 Dealers say the the krona's steep descent recently triggered Riksbank intervention, and according to traders the Riksbank has been in the market several times buying kronor against the mark at the 4.53, 4.54, and 4.55 kronor per mark levels in good volumes.
